Name: affect_labeling_debiasing
Title: Name It to Tame It: Does an LLM's Own Affect-Labeling Decouple Its Reasoning From Emotional Content?
Short Hypothesis: The human 'affect labeling' effect — putting a feeling into a compact emotion word incidentally dampens its influence on judgment — transfers to LLMs: requiring a model to first name the emotional content of an affect-laden input causally reduces the emotion's distorting pull on its subsequent reasoning (fewer affect-driven errors, better calibration on affective content), and this debiasing is mediated by a locatable affect-representation whose engagement drops after labeling and can be causally steered.
Related Work: Human affect-labeling research shows that verbally labeling an emotion incidentally (without intentional reappraisal) reduces amygdala/limbic responses and self-reported distress, distinct from and cheaper than reappraisal (Torre & Lieberman meta-analysis; Burklund et al. 2014, 116 cites; Lieberman fMRI/ERP, third-person self-talk 2017, 111 cites; Brooks et al. neuroimaging meta-analysis 2016, 128 cites), and that labeling in a second language further increases emotional distance (Morawetz et al. 2017). In LLMs, prior work studies emotion INJECTION and control — emotion vectors and steering (From Rational Answers to Emotional Resonance 2025; The Inner Sentiments of a Thought 2023), mechanistic localization of emotion inference to mid layers with appraisal-theory structure (Mechanistic Interpretability of Emotion Inference 2025), stress affecting performance (StressPrompt 2024), and emotion mediating Theory-of-Mind steering (Decomposing Theory of Mind 2025). ALL of this treats emotion as a signal to inject, detect, or amplify. NONE test the OPPOSITE, regulatory direction: whether the model's own act of labeling the emotional content of a stimulus causally REDUCES the emotion's downstream influence on reasoning/judgment (affect-labeling debiasing), whether this beats reappraisal-style prompting, or whether it is mediated by a locatable affect representation that labeling deflates. My prior proposals covered dual-process gears, foreign-language honesty, verbal overshadowing, and pragmatic enrichment, but never affect labeling as a self-regulation/debiasing mechanism. We uniquely transfer a robust human emotion-regulation finding into LLMs as a controlled label-then-judge intervention with a Location + Causal Intervention account and a high-stakes clinical/moral instance. Novelty locus: the phenomenon is that a robust human emotion-regulation effect (incidental affect labeling) transfers to LLMs; the primary contribution is the CAUSAL test of the direction OPPOSITE to all prior emotion work — where that work injects, detects, or amplifies emotion, we test whether the model NAMING the emotion REDUCES its downstream influence on reasoning — together with a mechanistic mediation account. This is distinct from generic sentiment detection, which reads emotion but does not regulate it, and it is not offered as a benchmark contribution. We treat 'mediated by an affect representation' as a hypothesis adjudicated by a pre-registered mediation-plus-steering chain, not asserted as a standard probing result.
Abstract: In humans, simply putting a feeling into a word — affect labeling — incidentally weakens that feeling's grip on judgment, dampening limbic responses without any intentional attempt to reinterpret the situation. We ask whether this regulatory relationship between language and cognition transfers to large language models: does requiring a model to first name the emotional content of an affect-laden input causally reduce the emotion's distorting influence on its subsequent reasoning? We assemble tasks where affect is designed to bias judgment away from the correct answer — emotionally charged framings of factual and probability questions, morally provocative dilemmas, sentiment-loaded evaluations, and emotionally distressing clinical vignettes — each with a labeled affect-driven error lure. Holding content constant, we compare four conditions: direct judgment; AFFECT-LABEL (name the emotion present before answering); a length-matched NON-AFFECT LABEL control (describe a non-emotional attribute); and reappraisal-style prompting. We predict an affect-labeling debiasing effect: labeling the emotion reduces affect-driven errors and improves calibration relative to direct and non-affect controls, is selective to affect-biased items, and matches or exceeds costlier reappraisal — mirroring the human incidental-regulation finding. Mechanistically, we locate an affect-representation via probing, test whether it is engaged during direct judgment and DEFLATED after the model labels the emotion (mediating the behavioral debiasing), and causally steer it: subtracting it should mimic labeling's benefit, amplifying it should reinstate affect-driven errors. Across several open-weight models we quantify the effect, its selectivity, its mechanistic mediation, and a high-stakes clinical instance where emotional framing silently biases triage. Our work reframes emotion words from something LLMs express into a tool that regulates their own reasoning. If the effect holds, affect-labeling becomes a simple, general debiasing prompt wherever LLMs process emotionally framed inputs — content moderation, mental-health and crisis chat, customer-support escalation, and moral/triage decision support — changing behavior by inserting one cheap label-then-judge step instead of costlier reappraisal or fine-tuning. If it is null, that is equally informative: it would dissociate LLMs from the human incidental affect-labeling mechanism and bound how far human emotion-regulation findings transfer to machine reasoning. We release the paired affect-biased judgment battery to support replication.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Affect-labeling debiasing is real, selective, and competitive with reappraisal): Tests the behavioral core - that requiring the model to name the emotion first reduces affect-driven errors and improves calibration, selectively on affect-biased items, at or below the cost of reappraisal. Data: a constructed affect-biased judgment battery of four families, ~250 items each (~1000 total), each authored as a matched pair - an AFFECT framing carrying a labeled affect-congruent lure, and a content-identical NEUTRAL framing with the affect stripped. Families and their seed sources: (a) emotionally charged factual/probability questions re-framed from TruthfulQA-style factual claims and calibration items; (b) morally provocative dilemmas adapted from the ETHICS and Moral Stories corpora; (c) sentiment-loaded truth judgments wrapping FEVER-style claims in strongly valenced language; (d) emotionally distressing clinical vignettes adapted from MedQA/MedMCQA stems. We author rather than harvest because no existing set holds content constant while toggling only affect; 250/family keeps two-annotator verification of meaning-preservation and lure validity (target >=90% agreement) affordable while giving ~1000 paired items for adequately powered mixed-effects estimation. Ground truth and the affect-congruent lure are auto-checkable. Models: Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Gemma-2-9B, all open-weight and run frozen (inference only, no weights trained here); decoding at temperature 0.7, 5 samples/item, 3 seeds (13/21/42). Conditions, content held constant with output format enforced and compliance verified: (i) DIRECT; (ii) AFFECT-LABEL (name the emotion(s) present before answering); (iii) NON-AFFECT LABEL (describe a length-matched non-emotional attribute - topic/entities - before answering); (iv) REAPPRAISAL prompting; (v) SECOND-LANGUAGE AFFECT-LABEL (name the emotion in a non-dominant language). Decisive metric: affect-driven-lure rate on AFFECT items (fraction of responses equal to the labeled affect-congruent wrong answer), modeled as lure_rate ~ condition*affect_status + (1|model) + (1|item). Secondary: expected calibration error (ECE) on the factual/probability family; token cost. Convincing result: AFFECT-LABEL lowers the affect-lure rate on AFFECT items by >=8 percentage points (pp) absolute versus NON-AFFECT LABEL with the condition x affect_status interaction 95% CI excluding 0 (the drop is specific to affect items, near-zero on neutral controls), reduces ECE by >=3 pp, and lands within 2 pp of - or better than - REAPPRAISAL at lower token cost. Indecision band: a 3-8 pp lure-rate reduction, or an interaction CI that grazes 0 - a directional but underpowered effect; landing here means labeling shows the predicted sign but the debiasing is not established, and we report it as suggestive and pool across models for power. Negative result: <3 pp reduction, or no larger effect than NON-AFFECT LABEL (interaction CI centered on 0) - this dissociates LLMs from the human incidental affect-labeling mechanism, indicating emotional influence on LLM judgment is not regulated by naming. The SECOND-LANGUAGE arm is exploratory: a further reduction corroborates the L2-distancing analogue, but its absence does not by itself refute H1.

Experiment 2 (H2 - A locatable affect representation): Tests that an affect-intensity signal is linearly decodable and separable from generic content. Data: hidden states collected on the same ~1000 paired items (AFFECT vs NEUTRAL framings, and pre- vs post-label token positions), 70/30 item-disjoint train/test split so no item appears in both. Model/protocol: the same five frozen models; a logistic linear probe (L2-regularized, 3 training seeds) trained per layer to decode affect presence/intensity; a difference-in-means affect-intensity direction derived from AFFECT-minus-NEUTRAL contrasts. Decisive metric: held-out per-layer AUROC of the affect probe (chance 0.5). Convincing result: best-layer held-out AUROC >=0.80 (expected mid-network, consistent with prior emotion-inference localization), with the difference-in-means direction reproducing >=0.75 AUROC, establishing a real, generalizing affect representation. Indecision band: best-layer AUROC 0.65-0.80 - a weak signal that supports mediation/steering only tentatively. Negative result: AUROC <0.65 anywhere - no separable affect representation, undercutting the mechanistic half of the hypothesis regardless of the behavioral outcome.

Experiment 3 (H3 - Labeling deflates the affect representation and this mediates the behavioral effect): Tests that naming the emotion reduces engagement of the affect direction at the judgment position, and that this reduction predicts fewer affect-driven errors. Data/protocol: for each AFFECT item, project the judgment-position hidden state onto the Exp-2 affect direction under DIRECT, AFFECT-LABEL, and NON-AFFECT LABEL; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: paired within-item drop in affect-direction engagement (AFFECT-LABEL minus DIRECT), and the Spearman correlation between per-item engagement drop and per-item reduction in affect-driven errors. Convincing result: engagement drops significantly after AFFECT-LABEL (paired effect, 95% CI excluding 0) but not after NON-AFFECT LABEL (CI including 0), and the mediation correlation |rho| >=0.30 with CI excluding 0, with a mediation model showing the engagement drop accounts for a substantial share of the condition->accuracy effect. Indecision band: |rho| 0.15-0.30, or a drop after AFFECT-LABEL that is not reliably larger than after NON-AFFECT LABEL - engagement moves but mediation is unproven. Negative result: |rho| <0.15 or no differential drop - labeling's behavioral benefit (if any) is not carried by deflation of this affect representation, breaking the proposed mechanistic chain.

Experiment 4 (H4 - The affect representation is causally steerable): Tests that subtracting the affect direction mimics labeling's benefit and that adding it reinstates affect-driven errors. Data/protocol: activation steering along the Exp-2 affect direction at the best mediating layer during DIRECT judgment (subtract) and after AFFECT-LABEL (add), across 4 coefficients spanning a dose ladder; controls are a random-direction vector of matched norm and no-steer; same five frozen models; specificity tracked on NEUTRAL items and via output perplexity/fluency. Decisive metric: change in affect-driven-lure rate under steering versus no-steer. Convincing result: subtracting the affect direction lowers the affect-lure rate by >=6 pp on DIRECT AFFECT items with a monotonic dose-response, adding it after AFFECT-LABEL reinstates the lure by >=6 pp, the random-direction control moves it <2 pp, and NEUTRAL-item accuracy and fluency stay within a pre-set 2 pp / small-perplexity tolerance. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp steering effect, or a non-monotonic dose - a causal contribution that is present but not cleanly attributable to this direction. Negative result: <2 pp effect, or an effect no larger than the random-direction control, or one that only appears alongside broken fluency - the affect representation is not causally load-bearing for the debiasing.

Experiment 5 (H1/H4 - High-stakes clinical instance): Tests whether emotional framing biases triage and whether affect-labeling and affect-direction steering reduce that bias where it matters. Data: ~250 triage vignettes (subset/extension of family (d)) holding identical clinical facts while varying only the emotional framing of the patient/family, each with a labeled correct urgency/triage decision and a framing-driven error. Model/protocol: same five frozen models; compare DIRECT, AFFECT-LABEL, and subtract-affect-direction steering; report on the fine-distinction subset where framing and correct decision diverge; aggregate reporting only. Decisive metric: framing-driven triage-error rate on fine-distinction cases. Convincing result: AFFECT-LABEL and/or affect-subtraction steering cut the framing-driven error rate by >=6 pp versus DIRECT with CI excluding 0, without lowering accuracy on neutrally framed matched cases. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp reduction - a safety-relevant but modest effect warranting replication before any deployment claim. Negative result: <2 pp reduction - the regulation demonstrated in Experiments 1-4 does not transfer to a realistic high-stakes decision, bounding the practical reach of the mechanism.

Cross-experiment controls and reporting: all effects are reported as mixed-effects estimates with 95% CIs against the pre-registered effect-size thresholds stated above (and pre-registered as the confirmatory comparisons AFFECT-LABEL vs DIRECT, vs NON-AFFECT LABEL, and vs REAPPRAISAL, so a positive result cannot be read as mere 'extra deliberation helps'). We add a NEGATIVE-CONTROL condition in which emotion words are present but decision-irrelevant (the affect-congruent answer is NOT the lure), where affect-labeling should confer no benefit — establishing that any debiasing is selective to affect that actually biases the judgment rather than to the mere presence of emotion words. We report results split by task family, model family (base vs instruction-tuned), and prompt format to map robustness and boundary conditions.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Affect-labeling may help simply by adding a pre-answer reasoning step / more tokens rather than via naming the emotion; mitigated by the length-matched NON-AFFECT LABEL control (equal pre-answer description, no emotion naming) and by testing the affect-specific selectivity interaction rather than raw gains. (2) Instruction-tuned models may already discount emotional framing, muting the debiasing effect (ceiling); we include harder/more vivid framings, base variants, multiple models, and measure calibration where headroom is larger. (3) 'Affect-driven lure' items may conflate emotional bias with general difficulty; matched neutral-framing controls (same content, affect removed) isolate the affect contribution, and the lure error signature (errors are the SPECIFIC affect-congruent answer) distinguishes genuine affect bias from random error. (4) The affect direction may entangle with generic content/sentiment or difficulty rather than a regulatable affect-intensity signal; mitigated by matched affect/neutral contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and neutral-item specificity checks. (5) Reappraisal is a strong, cheap prompt baseline that may match affect-labeling; a finding that labeling merely matches reappraisal at lower cost, or that a located affect direction mediates both, is still informative about the mechanism. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (labeling the emotion does not reduce affect's influence, or does so no more than non-affect labeling) is itself informative: it would dissociate LLMs from the human incidental affect-labeling mechanism, indicating emotional influence on LLM judgment is not regulated by naming. (8) The affect-labeling framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like emotional experience; clinical/moral experiments are run in controlled research settings and reported only in aggregate.

Name: curse_of_knowledge_teaching
Title: The Curse of Knowledge in LLMs: Is Explanation Quality Causally Gated by an Internal Model of the Learner?
Short Hypothesis: LLMs exhibit a curse of knowledge: by default they produce audience-agnostic explanations pitched near their own knowledge level rather than the learner's, so their teaching underperforms; explanation quality is causally gated by whether the model first forms and uses an internal representation of the learner's knowledge state (a 'learner model'), and this learner model is locatable and steerable, so amplifying it improves how much a downstream learner actually learns while suppressing it reproduces expert-blind explanations.
Related Work: Cognitive science and neuroscience establish the Prediction-Transmission hypothesis: effective human teachers first predict a learner's knowledge state via mentalizing (Theory of Mind) and then select what to say, with teaching quality tracked by mentalizing regions (Teachers recruit mentalizing regions, 2023; Enhancement of teaching outcome through neural prediction of students' knowledge state, 2018; utility-based Bayesian-ToM teachers, 2023; mentalizing-vs-heuristics in teaching, 2024/2025). The 'curse of knowledge' / expert blind spot is a robust human bias where knowing something impairs adapting to a novice. In LLMs, interpretability work shows belief/ToM representations exist and are steerable (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others, 2024; Decomposing Theory of Mind, 2025; Emergent Social World Models, 2026), and audience-design theory formalizes tailoring speech to listeners (Toward a Comprehensive Theory of Audience Design, 2012). However, ALL LLM-teaching work is applied (personalized tutoring systems) or ToM-in-comprehension; NONE (a) test whether an LLM's own explanations suffer a curse of knowledge that measurably reduces downstream learner gains, (b) test whether teaching quality is CAUSALLY gated by an internal learner-knowledge-state representation the model forms before explaining, or (c) locate and steer that learner model to causally improve or degrade teaching effectiveness measured by actual learner learning. We uniquely transfer the Prediction-Transmission hypothesis and the curse of knowledge into LLMs with a Location + Causal Intervention account and a high-stakes patient-education instance. Novelty locus: prior LLM-teaching benchmarks (e.g., EducationQ, PEARL) and mentalizing-in-teaching studies (e.g., 'Do LLMs Mentalize When They Teach?') measure tutoring quality or ToM in comprehension but never (a) score explanations by an independent learner's downstream gain, (b) test that this quality is CAUSALLY gated by an internal learner-knowledge representation the model forms before explaining, or (c) locate and steer that representation to raise or degrade actual learning — the exact behavioral gap their metrics cannot reach. The problem-definition delta is 'default audience-agnostic explanations pitched near the model's own knowledge' versus 'teaching that first infers and conditions on the learner's knowledge state.' That teaching can worsen as teacher competence rises is reported as a new result in this setting, not a new theory of expert blind spots.
Abstract: Good teaching is an act of audience design: effective human teachers first predict what a learner already knows, then tailor their explanation, and teaching outcomes track this predictive, mentalizing step. Humans who know a subject also suffer a 'curse of knowledge' that makes them explain past novices. We ask whether large language models, whose intelligence is expressed through language, teach well or fall prey to the same curse, and whether their teaching is causally driven by an internal model of the learner. We measure teaching effectiveness the way cognitive scientists do: an explanation is good to the extent that an independent, simulated learner who reads it then answers downstream questions correctly. We make three claims. First, the curse of knowledge is real: by default LLMs produce explanations pitched near their own knowledge level, and forcing them to first infer and state the learner's knowledge state (a prediction step) improves downstream learner gains, especially for low-knowledge learners, while offering little benefit for expert learners. Second, teaching quality is diagnostic of an internal learner model: a probe can decode the learner's inferred knowledge level from the teacher model's hidden states before it explains, and how accurately it does so predicts explanation effectiveness. Third, the learner model is causal and steerable: steering along a located 'learner-knowledge-level' direction shifts explanations up or down the expertise gradient and changes how much the learner actually learns, while suppressing it reproduces expert-blind explanations. We evaluate across several open-weight models and knowledge domains, plus a high-stakes patient-education instance where a curse-of-knowledge explanation leaves a lay patient misinformed. Our work reframes language as audience design and teaching quality as gated by an internal model of the mind being taught. Beyond patient education, the same audience-design failure bears on classroom tutoring, customer support, and workplace training; we treat a >=5 pp change in downstream learning gain as the threshold that would justify revising how LLM tutors are prompted and evaluated. We separate the phenomenon (a behavioral warning that stronger models can teach worse) from the fix (causal learner-model steering), since different audiences would adopt each. If null — LLMs already audience-design adequately and teaching is not gated by an internal learner model — that too informs how tutoring systems and their benchmarks should be built.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - The curse of knowledge is real and predict-then-teach relieves it): Tests that default LLM explanations are pitched too high and that forcing the model to first infer the learner's knowledge state improves how much an independent learner actually learns, selectively for low-knowledge learners. Data: a constructed teaching set over four domains, ~150 topics each (~600 topics), every topic paired with 5-8 held-out downstream comprehension questions. Seed sources: elementary science (topics/questions adapted from the ARC and OpenBookQA science-question pools), statistics/probability (authored), one technical CS concept family (authored from standard curricula), and medicine (adapted from MedQA/MedMCQA stems). We author/adapt because teaching-effectiveness measurement needs topic-linked downstream question sets that off-the-shelf QA lacks; 150/domain balances two-annotator question-validity checking against power. Learner personas span a knowledge gradient (novice/intermediate/expert) via short profiles. Models: TEACHER in {Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Gemma-2-9B}, all frozen; LEARNER is a separate, different-family/smaller panel {Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-2-2B}, also frozen, to avoid teacher=learner shared-bias; decoding temperature 0.7, 3 seeds (13/21/42). Conditions (content held constant): (i) DEFAULT (topic only, no learner info); (ii) LEARNER-AWARE (persona provided); (iii) PREDICT-THEN-TEACH (model first states the learner's likely prior knowledge, then explains); (iv) length-matched NON-AUDIENCE reflection control (reflect on the topic's structure). Decisive metric: learner downstream accuracy gain over a no-explanation baseline (learner answers the same questions with no explanation), modeled as learner_gain ~ teaching_condition*learner_level + (1|teacher) + (1|topic). Secondary: objective explanation level (readability grade, count of presupposed/undefined concepts). Convincing result: PREDICT-THEN-TEACH raises novice-learner gain by >=5 pp over DEFAULT with the condition x learner_level interaction 95% CI excluding 0 (novices benefit, expert-learner gain unchanged within +/-2 pp), beats the NON-AUDIENCE control by >=3 pp, and DEFAULT explanations sit objectively near expert level (readability/presupposed-concept counts above the novice-appropriate threshold) - the curse signature. Indecision band: a 2-5 pp novice gain, or an interaction CI grazing 0 - audience design helps directionally but is not established over mere extra deliberation. Negative result: <2 pp gain, or no advantage over the NON-AUDIENCE control - LLMs already audience-design adequately and teaching quality is not gated by an explicit prediction step.

Experiment 2 (H1 - The curse scales with teacher expertise): Tests the counterintuitive prediction that a teacher model explains worse to novices on topics it knows better. Data/protocol: the same ~600 topics; per topic estimate teacher topic-competence (its own solve rate / logit margin) and compute the novice-learner effectiveness gap (DEFAULT novice gain minus expert gain); same five frozen teachers and learner panel. Decisive metric: Spearman correlation between teacher topic-competence and the novice effectiveness gap. Convincing result: rho >=0.30 with 95% CI excluding 0 - higher teacher competence predicts a larger novice penalty, the expert-blind-spot signature. Indecision band: rho 0.15-0.30 - a weak trend. Negative result: rho <0.15 or CI including 0 - the curse magnitude is independent of teacher expertise, weakening the human-analogy framing while leaving Experiment 1's core intact.

Experiment 3 (H2 - A locatable learner model predicts teaching quality): Tests that the learner's inferred knowledge level is linearly decodable from teacher hidden states before it explains and that decodability predicts effectiveness. Data: teacher hidden states at the pre-explanation position on LEARNER-AWARE and PREDICT-THEN-TEACH trials across all topics; 70/30 topic-disjoint split. Protocol: per-layer L2-regularized linear probe (3 seeds) decoding the learner's specified/inferred level (novice/expert); same five frozen teachers. Decisive metric: held-out per-layer AUROC for novice-vs-expert learner level (chance 0.5). Convincing result: best-layer AUROC >=0.80, probe-decoded learner-level predicts per-topic teaching effectiveness (rho >=0.30, CI excluding 0), and on DEFAULT trials the probe reads a near-expert default audience - direct evidence the model assumes an expert reader. Indecision band: AUROC 0.65-0.80, or effectiveness correlation rho 0.15-0.30 - a learner representation exists but its link to teaching quality is tentative. Negative result: AUROC <0.65 - no decodable learner model, so teaching quality cannot be attributed to one.

Experiment 4 (H3 - The learner model is causal and steerable): Tests that steering a learner-knowledge-level direction shifts explanation level and actual learner gains, with mediation. Data/protocol: derive a difference-in-means learner-knowledge-level direction (novice-minus-expert learner-model contrasts); steer -direction (toward novice) on DEFAULT explanations and +direction (toward expert) across 4 coefficients; controls random-direction and no-steer; same five frozen teachers and learner panel; specificity tracked on expert-learner gains and fluency. Decisive metric: change in novice-learner gain under steering versus no-steer. Convincing result: novice-ward steering lowers presupposed-concept counts and raises novice-learner gain by >=4 pp with monotonic dose-response, expert-ward steering reproduces expert-blind explanations that reduce novice gain, random-direction moves gain <1.5 pp, expert-learner gain and fluency preserved, and steering-induced change in the Exp-3 learner-level probe predicts the change in learner gain (mediation, CI excluding 0). Indecision band: a 1.5-4 pp steering effect or absent mediation - a causal contribution that is present but not clearly routed through the learner representation. Negative result: <1.5 pp effect or no better than random-direction - the learner-level direction is not causally load-bearing for teaching quality.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 - High-stakes patient-education instance): Tests whether default explanations leave a lay patient unable to answer safety-critical questions and whether predict-then-teach and novice steering fix it. Data: ~150 diagnosis/medication-regimen topics (medicine domain subset/extension), each with safety-critical comprehension/action questions (e.g., when to take a drug, warning signs), targeted at a lay-patient learner persona. Protocol: same five frozen teachers, lay-patient learner persona from the panel; compare DEFAULT, PREDICT-THEN-TEACH, and novice-ward steering on the fine-distinction subset; aggregate reporting only. Decisive metric: safety-critical comprehension/action failure rate of the lay-patient learner. Convincing result: PREDICT-THEN-TEACH and/or novice steering cut the safety-critical failure rate by >=6 pp versus DEFAULT (CI excluding 0) without reducing accuracy for an expert-clinician learner on the same material. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp reduction - safety-relevant but modest. Negative result: <2 pp reduction - the audience-design benefit does not transfer to high-stakes patient education, bounding its practical value. Robustness across the whole battery: multiple independent learner models guard against shared-bias artifacts, and a small human-learner validation on a random subset checks that model-learner gains track human-learner gains.

Baselines and leakage safety: the primary suite compares PREDICT-THEN-TEACH against prompt-only audience design, length-matched non-audience reflection, generic simplification, and self-consistency, so gains cannot be attributed to verbosity or extra tokens alone; downstream comprehension questions are authored/held out separately from the explanations and checked to be leakage-safe (not answerable from the topic prompt alone); and every effect is reported as a mixed-effects estimate with 95% CIs and the pre-registered null for the novice/expert interaction, probe AUROC, and steering effect stated per experiment.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Using an LLM as the simulated learner risks shared-bias artifacts (teacher and learner fail on the same items); mitigated by using multiple, weaker/different-family learner models, by measuring gain over a no-explanation baseline (isolating the explanation's contribution), and by a small human-learner validation on a subset. (2) PREDICT-THEN-TEACH may help simply by adding pre-explanation reasoning tokens rather than genuine audience modeling; the length-matched NON-AUDIENCE reflection control and the learner-level x condition selectivity (helps novices, not experts) isolate audience design from mere extra deliberation. (3) The curse may be small if instruction-tuned models already adapt to explicit personas; we include the DEFAULT (no persona) condition where the curse should be strongest, harder technical topics, and measure objective explanation level, and a null there is still informative. (4) The learner-knowledge-level direction may entangle with generic simplicity/verbosity rather than a genuine learner model; mitigated by matched novice/expert learner-model contrasts (same topic), held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and the mediation test linking probe change to learner-gain change. (5) Teaching-effectiveness measurement is noisy and depends on downstream-question design; we use multiple questions per topic, report CIs, and validate against human learners. (6) Effects may be small or model/domain-specific; we test multiple models and domains and report effect sizes. (7) A null result (LLMs already audience-design optimally, no curse, teaching quality independent of an internal learner model) is itself informative, indicating LLM explanation is not gated by mentalizing the learner. (8) The curse-of-knowledge / Prediction-Transmission framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like pedagogical intent; patient-education experiments are run in controlled research settings with only aggregate reporting.

Name: strategic_vagueness_escape_hatch
Title: The Vagueness Escape Hatch: Do LLMs Strategically Underspecify Their Answers to Avoid Being Wrong, Masking Knowledge They Actually Have?
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM anticipates that committing to a specific answer risks being wrong, it does not simply reason harder or say 'I don't know' — it strategically lowers the SEMANTIC SPECIFICITY of its output (hedging, generalities, non-answers) as a self-protective escape hatch, and this vagueness masks decision-relevant knowledge the model demonstrably has; the degree of self-protective vagueness is a locatable, steerable internal signal distinct from verbalized confidence, and suppressing it recovers correct specific answers the model was otherwise hiding.
Related Work: Prior work shows verbal uncertainty is a single linear feature only moderately correlated with semantic uncertainty and can be calibrated to reduce overconfident hallucination (Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty as a Linear Feature, 2025), that models can verbalize calibrated confidence (Teaching Models to Express Uncertainty, 2022), and that ambiguity is sparsely encoded and steers answering-vs-abstention (Sparse Neurons Carry Signals of Question Ambiguity, 2025). Loophole work shows models strategically exploit ambiguity when goals conflict (LMs Identify Ambiguities and Exploit Loopholes, 2025), and semantic-underspecification reviews note humans use underspecification strategically for efficiency while LLMs overcommit to deterministic readings (Bridging Philosophical Foundations, 2025; Dealing with Semantic Underspecification, 2023). ALL existing work treats output vagueness/uncertainty either as (a) a confidence LABEL to calibrate, (b) an INPUT-ambiguity property, or (c) an abstention decision. NONE treat the SEMANTIC SPECIFICITY of the answer CONTENT itself as a self-protective, difficulty-gated strategy that trades commitment for error-avoidance, tests whether this vagueness MASKS knowledge the model actually has, or provides a Location + Causal Intervention account showing suppression recovers hidden correct answers. My prior proposals covered verbalized-confidence calibration, ambiguity-branch collapse, difficulty-gated language-agnostic steering, and honesty, but none address strategic OUTPUT underspecification as a knowledge-masking escape hatch. We uniquely reframe answer vagueness from a calibration signal into a controllable escape hatch with a high-stakes clinical/legal instance. Novelty locus, as one-row deltas against the closest families: versus verbal-uncertainty-feature/calibration work the output variable is answer-content specificity (not a confidence label); versus abstention it is graded underspecification (not a binary refuse/answer); versus input-ambiguity work the ambiguity is self-generated, not in the question; versus 'knowing but not showing' the observable is a Knowledge-Masking Gap and the intervention target is a commitment direction dissociated from the verbal-uncertainty feature. We use 'strategic' and 'self-protective' as behavioral shorthand for a difficulty-gated pattern, not a claim of deliberate optimization over explicit error costs.
Abstract: Large language models are known to sometimes hallucinate with unwarranted confidence, and much work aims to calibrate the confidence LABELS they attach to answers. We investigate the opposite, underexamined failure: strategic underspecification. We hypothesize that when a model anticipates that a specific answer is risky, it protects itself not by reasoning harder or honestly abstaining, but by lowering the SEMANTIC SPECIFICITY of the answer itself — retreating into hedges, generalities, and non-committal restatements — and that this vagueness masks decision-relevant knowledge the model actually possesses. We make three claims. First, the escape hatch is real and difficulty-gated: on questions where a specific answer is required, output specificity drops as anticipated error-risk rises, over and above genuine lack of knowledge. Second, vagueness masks knowledge: on many vague-answer trials, the model's correct specific answer is recoverable — via a forced-commitment prompt or via a probe on hidden states — showing the information was present but withheld. Third, the escape hatch is a locatable, steerable signal distinct from verbalized confidence: we identify a 'commitment/specificity' direction, show it is separable from the verbal-uncertainty feature, and steer it to make the model commit — recovering correct specific answers it was hiding — or to induce protective vagueness on questions it would otherwise answer. We evaluate across several open-weight models on factual QA, reasoning, and a high-stakes clinical/legal-advice instance where a vague non-answer looks safe but withholds needed guidance, quantifying the difficulty-gated vagueness effect, the knowledge-masking gap, and steering controllability. Concretely, the core claims are: (1) answer-content specificity is a difficulty-gated behavioral axis distinct from confidence wording and abstention; (2) reduced specificity rises with anticipated error-risk beyond genuine unknownness; (3) vague answers can mask recoverable correct knowledge (a Knowledge-Masking Gap); (4) a locatable, steerable commitment direction is separable from the verbal-uncertainty feature; (5) suppressing it recovers hidden answers without merely increasing recklessness. Anticipated error-risk is estimated EX ANTE from independent repeated-sampling accuracy, never from the response being scored, to avoid circularity. If confirmed, this shifts honesty evaluation from confidence labels and abstention toward semantic specificity and hidden-knowledge recovery, and motivates reward shaping and deployment monitoring that penalize knowledge-masking vagueness; if the gap collapses once knowledge and verbosity are controlled, it rules out a popular interpretive story about hedging. We compare base, instruction-tuned, and RLHF variants to test whether post-training amplifies or reduces masking, and report prevalence (how often masking occurs on realistic tasks) alongside effect sizes. We use 'strategic' as behavioral shorthand, not a claim of intent.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Output vagueness is difficulty-gated, beyond genuine unknownness, and selective): Tests that on questions demanding a specific answer, output specificity falls as anticipated error-risk rises even for questions the model knows, while genuinely-unanswerable items are appropriately vague. Data: a specificity-demanding battery, ~250 items each across four families (~1000 total): (a) short-answer factual QA (single correct entity/value) sampled from Natural Questions and TriviaQA; (b) multi-step reasoning with a definite answer (GSM8K-style); (c) recommendation/advice items (choose among N concrete options, authored); (d) a high-stakes clinical/legal-advice family requiring a specific action/dosage/ruling (adapted from MedQA and public legal-QA stems). Each item carries a labeled correct SPECIFIC answer and a labeled vague-escape response. Matched genuinely-unanswerable/ambiguous controls (~250) are drawn from SQuAD-2.0 unanswerables and known-unknown question sets, where vagueness is the correct behavior. We adapt existing QA where possible and author only the option/advice families; 250/family keeps human specificity-rating validation affordable. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; per-item anticipated error-risk estimated from 10-sample repeated-sampling accuracy at temperature 0.7; 3 seeds (13/21/42). Output-specificity metric (validated against human ratings on a 200-item sample, target rho >=0.7): a rubric classifier (names a concrete answer vs hedges/restates), hedge-marker density, and whether an entailment model can extract a definite answer. Decisive metric: regression slope of output specificity on anticipated error-risk for ANSWERABLE items, controlling for accuracy, modeled as specificity ~ error_risk + item_answerable + (1|model) + (1|item). Convincing result: slope <= -0.15 specificity-units per unit error-risk on answerable items with 95% CI excluding 0, the effect surviving covariation on accuracy (so vagueness is not merely tracking unknownness), and unanswerable controls staying appropriately vague (near-floor specificity) - the escape-hatch signature concentrated on high-risk-but-known items. Indecision band: slope -0.05 to -0.15, or a CI grazing 0 - a directional gating that is not clearly separable from genuine unknownness. Negative result: slope > -0.05 or CI including 0 - output vagueness tracks only genuine unknownness, i.e., honest under-specification rather than a self-protective strategy.

Experiment 2 (H2 - Vagueness masks knowledge the model actually has): Tests that on vague-answer trials the correct specific answer is recoverable, unlike on genuine-unknown items. Data/protocol: on the answerable-item vague-answer trials from Experiment 1, recover the latent answer two ways - (a) a FORCED-COMMITMENT reprompt ('give exactly one specific answer'), and (b) a held-out linear probe on the pre-answer hidden state decoding the correct specific answer (per-layer, 70/30 item-disjoint split, 3 seeds); same five frozen models. Decisive metric: the Knowledge-Masking Gap = fraction of vague-answer trials whose forced or probed answer is correct. Convincing result: Knowledge-Masking Gap >=25%, while forced-commitment on genuine-unknown items yields correct answers <10% (so the gap is not lucky guessing), and the pre-answer probe reaches AUROC/answer-recovery well above chance on the same trials - independent confirmation the information was present but withheld. Indecision band: gap 10-25% - some masked knowledge but not a dominant pattern. Negative result: gap <10%, or no better than the genuine-unknown baseline - vagueness reflects real lack of knowledge, refuting the masking claim.

Experiment 3 (H3a - A locatable commitment/specificity direction distinct from verbalized confidence): Tests that a specificity signal exists in hidden states and is separable from the known verbal-uncertainty feature (VUF). Data/protocol: difference-in-means commitment/specificity direction from specific-answer-minus-vague-answer contrasts (content-matched); the VUF re-derived per prior work; compare via cosine similarity and test incremental prediction of output specificity beyond VUF; same five frozen models, 70/30 split. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC of the commitment direction for predicting output specificity, and its incremental predictive value over VUF. Convincing result: commitment-direction AUROC >=0.75, cosine similarity with VUF <0.5, and the commitment direction adds significant prediction of output specificity beyond VUF (nested-model likelihood-ratio / delta-AUROC CI excluding 0) - establishing a distinct content-specificity signal. Indecision band: AUROC 0.65-0.75 or cosine 0.5-0.7 - a signal that partly overlaps VUF. Negative result: AUROC <0.65 or the direction collapses onto VUF (cosine >0.7, no incremental value) - there is no distinct commitment signal, only a confidence label.

Experiment 4 (H3b - Steering the commitment direction recovers hidden answers and induces vagueness, selectively): Tests causal control while preserving appropriate vagueness where warranted. Data/protocol: steer +commitment on vague-answer trials and -commitment on normally-answered items, 4 coefficients; controls random-direction and no-steer; same five frozen models; critical specificity check on the genuinely-unanswerable controls (steering must NOT force commitment there) and on clinical/legal unsafe-commitment risk. Decisive metric: fraction of vague-answer trials converted to a correct specific answer under +commitment steering (without increased error), versus no-steer/random. Convincing result: +commitment recovers a correct specific answer on >=6 pp more vague trials than no-steer with monotonic dose-response, -commitment induces protective vagueness on >=6 pp of previously-answered items, random-direction moves <2 pp, and on unanswerable controls +commitment does NOT raise inappropriate commitment (stays within a 2 pp tolerance) with fluency preserved. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp effect, or recovery that comes with rising error on unanswerable controls - causal but not cleanly beneficial. Negative result: <2 pp effect or no better than random - the commitment direction is not causally load-bearing for output specificity.

Experiment 5 (H1-H3 - High-stakes clinical/legal instance): Tests that safe-looking vague non-answers withhold guidance the model has, and that commitment steering recovers it without unsafe over-commitment. Data: the ~250 clinical/legal-advice items requiring a specific action, split into cases the model demonstrably knows (via forced-commitment/probe) versus genuinely uncertain. Protocol: same five frozen models; measure unhelpful-vague-non-answer rate on known cases and, under +commitment steering, conversion to correct specific guidance versus induced unsafe commitment on uncertain cases; aggregate reporting only. Decisive metric: rate of unhelpful vague non-answers on demonstrably-known cases, and the net helpful-minus-unsafe change under steering. Convincing result: on known cases, >=15% of responses are unhelpfully vague despite recoverable knowledge, and +commitment steering converts >=6 pp of these into correct specific guidance while raising unsafe commitment on genuinely-uncertain cases by <2 pp. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp helpful conversion, or unsafe-commitment rise in the 2-4 pp range - a favorable but not clearly net-positive trade. Negative result: no meaningful vague-but-known rate, or steering trades helpfulness for equal unsafe commitment - the escape hatch is not a controllable, safely-correctable failure in this setting.

Masking-gap baselines and probe hygiene: the forced-commitment recovery in Experiment 2 is compared against temperature-matched second-sample, majority-vote, and answer-space-constrained guessing baselines so the gap is not inflated by lucky guessing; the hidden-state probe uses strict item/template-disjoint splits and reports calibration (not only accuracy) to guard against overfitting; the specificity metric is reported alongside verbosity/length/register controls, including adversarial long-but-vague and short-but-specific items; and the commitment-direction causal tests include verbal-uncertainty-feature subtraction, orthogonalization, matched-norm interventions, and checks on unrelated capabilities. All results are reported with 95% CIs and per-task/per-model mixed-effects models rather than single thresholds.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Vagueness may reflect genuine lack of knowledge rather than strategic self-protection; mitigated by the Knowledge-Masking Gap (forcing/probing must recover the CORRECT specific answer, not a random guess) and by the genuinely-unanswerable controls where forcing should NOT recover correct answers. (2) Automatic specificity scoring is noisy; we use multiple metrics (classifier, hedge density, entailment-extractability) plus human validation. (3) Forced-commitment reprompting could induce lucky guessing that inflates the masking gap; we compare against genuine-unknown items (where forcing yields wrong answers) and require the hidden-state probe to independently confirm latent knowledge. (4) The commitment/specificity direction may entangle with the verbal-uncertainty feature or generic difficulty; mitigated by explicit dissociation from VUF, matched specific/vague contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and unanswerable-item specificity checks. (5) Instruction-tuned/safety-aligned models may hedge for alignment reasons rather than error-avoidance; we test base variants, separate alignment-driven from risk-driven vagueness via the difficulty-gating analysis, and report both. (6) A good intervention must not become recklessly committal; we explicitly measure that steering preserves appropriate vagueness on genuinely uncertain items and does not raise unsafe commitment in the clinical/legal setting. (7) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (8) A null result (vagueness tracks only genuine unknownness, no masking gap, no distinct steerable signal) is itself informative, indicating LLM output vagueness is honest under-specification rather than a self-protective escape hatch. (9) The 'escape hatch' framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like intent; high-stakes experiments run in controlled research settings with aggregate reporting only.

Name: polarity_load_tracking
Title: Carrying the 'Not': Does Tracking Active Negations Impose a Compounding Working-Memory Load on LLM Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: An LLM represents a negated proposition as a positive proposition plus an approximately additive, separable 'polarity flag' (an operational hypothesis we test against rival encodings), so that reasoning which must hold and propagate multiple active negations across steps degrades with the NUMBER of live negations (a compounding polarity load), independent of surface length or difficulty; this polarity load is a locatable, steerable internal quantity, and errors are dominated by polarity-drop failures (silently reverting a negated fact to its positive) that can be causally reduced by amplifying the polarity signal.
Related Work: Prior negation work is overwhelmingly about single-sentence UNDERSTANDING: NLI and cloze failures on negation (MoNLI 2020; Negation/Coordination/Quantifiers 2022; CONDAQA 2022; ScoNe 2023; Pink Elephant 2025), theoretical 'strong hallucinations' from negation as a latent operator (2024), and localization of negation to early text-encoder layers (BERT attention 2020; CLIP negation 2024; NAST 2026). Reasoning-focused work shows CoT is not robust to lexical negation on single syllogisms (2023) and that symbolic cues including negation destabilize early-layer attention and drive hallucination (2026). ALL of this treats a fixed, typically small number of negations per item and studies comprehension or single-step inference. NONE frame the NUMBER of simultaneously ACTIVE negations that must be held and propagated across a multi-step reasoning chain as a graded working-memory-like LOAD with a compounding accuracy penalty, none isolate a 'polarity-drop' error mode (reverting a negated fact to positive mid-chain), and none give a Location + Causal Intervention account of a separable, additive polarity signal that can be steered to relieve the load. My prior proposals covered information-density pacing, register shift, ambiguity-branch collapse, and pragmatic enrichment, but never negation/polarity tracking as a reasoning load. We uniquely reframe negation from a comprehension deficit into a compounding, mechanistically-characterized reasoning-load phenomenon with a high-stakes clinical instance. Novelty locus: the contribution is a mechanistic package — active-negation-count scaling of a compounding load, an approximately additive polarity representation, a polarity-drop error signature, and causal rescue/induction — plus a released active-negation-load benchmark and analysis tools, not merely the observation that negation is hard. Delta versus the closest families: multi-hop cognitive-load work varies reasoning depth but never the number of live negations at fixed depth; negation-probing and negation-forgetting work study single-sentence comprehension, never a graded cross-step propagation load with a drop signature. Negation propagation also matters beyond clinical text — in legal and policy conditions, retrieval filters, and agent-planning constraints — where a dropped 'not' silently flips a decision.
Abstract: Negation is trivial to state and notoriously hard for language models, but existing work studies it as a single-sentence comprehension problem. We ask a different question central to how language bounds machine intelligence: what does it cost an LLM to CARRY negations through multi-step reasoning? We hypothesize that a model encodes a negated proposition as its positive counterpart plus a separable, additive polarity flag, so that reasoning which must simultaneously hold and propagate several live negations pays a compounding cost: accuracy falls with the number of active negations, over and above surface length and problem difficulty, and failures are dominated by 'polarity drops' in which a negated fact silently reverts to positive partway through the chain. We make three claims. First, the load is real and graded: on reasoning chains where we vary only how many propositions are negated (content and length matched), accuracy declines with negation count and errors concentrate on dropped-polarity conclusions. Second, polarity is a separable, locatable quantity: a probe decodes each proposition's live polarity from hidden states mid-chain, its decodability degrades as negation load rises, and this degradation predicts polarity-drop errors before they surface. Third, the load is causally relievable: steering along a located 'polarity' direction (or patching the pre-drop polarity representation) restores dropped negations and reduces errors, while suppressing it induces polarity drops even at low load. We evaluate across several open-weight models on logic, entailment chains, and multi-hop QA, plus a high-stakes clinical instance where a dropped 'no history of' or 'contraindicated' silently flips a decision, quantifying the compounding load, its polarity-drop signature, and mechanistic mediation. We release the negation-load battery (with matched double-negation and marker-free logically-equivalent controls) and the polarity probing/steering tools as reusable artifacts. We frame the additive-flag account as an operational hypothesis tested against rival explanations — generic difficulty, uncertainty/confidence collapse, surface 'not'-token tracking, training-frequency effects, and answer-content leakage — via matched controls and distinct predicted signatures. If confirmed, downstream reasoning evaluation and mitigation would treat negation count as a first-class load variable; if rejected, it would show negation is absorbed into content rather than carried as a separable flag.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - A compounding polarity load with a polarity-drop error signature): Tests that accuracy declines with the number of simultaneously active negations, beyond surface length and difficulty, and that errors concentrate on dropped-polarity conclusions rather than random failure. Data: a constructed negation-load battery, ~250 base items each across three families (~750 base items, ~3750 rendered): (a) deductive logic chains depth 3-6 over propositions, (b) entailment/consistency chains, (c) multi-hop QA over short passages. Each base item is rendered into a matched SET differing ONLY in how many of its propositions are negated (0/1/2/3/4 active negations) via minimal 'not'/'no' edits that preserve content, holding reasoning-step count, token length, and answer structure constant. Each item has a labeled correct answer AND a labeled POLARITY-DROP lure (the answer that follows if exactly one negated fact is treated as positive). A surface control adds equal-length non-negation modifiers. We construct because no existing set varies negation count while matching depth/length; 250 base items/family gives ~3750 rendered items for load-curve estimation and keeps entailment/human meaning-preservation checks affordable. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; greedy plus temperature-0.7 sampling, 3 seeds (13/21/42). Decisive metric: accuracy as a function of negation_count, modeled as accuracy ~ negation_count + chain_depth + token_length + (1|model) + (1|item); secondary polarity-drop-rate and the polarity-drop share of errors. Convincing result: accuracy declines monotonically (and super-additively) with negation_count beyond depth/length (per-negation coefficient CI excluding 0, e.g. >=4 pp accuracy loss per added active negation), the equal-length surface-modifier control shows <1 pp/modifier decline (isolating polarity from generic modifier load), and >=50% of errors on high-load items are the specific polarity-drop lure (the diagnostic that a negation was silently dropped). Indecision band: a 1.5-4 pp/negation decline, or a polarity-drop error share of 30-50% - a real but weak or not-clearly-polarity-shaped load. Negative result: <1.5 pp/negation and lure share near chance, or a surface-modifier control that declines just as much - no specific compounding polarity load, indicating negation is absorbed into content rather than a load-bearing flag.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Flag-based additivity: double-negation and error-localization): Tests the separable-additive-flag signature - that cancelling double-negations are easier than an equal count of independent negations, and that failures localize to a specific dropped negation. Data/protocol: within the same battery, matched double-negation items (surface 'not' present but live polarity positive) versus items with the same count of independent negations; per-item error-localization tracing the wrong final answer to a specific proposition whose polarity flipped; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: accuracy gap (double-negation minus equal-count independent-negation), and the error-localization rate (fraction of errors attributable to one identifiable dropped negation). Convincing result: double-negation accuracy exceeds equal-count independent-negation accuracy by >=6 pp (CI excluding 0) - consistent with flag cancellation rather than raw 'not'-token count - and error-localization succeeds on >=60% of errors. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp double-negation advantage, or localization 40-60% - suggestive of flag structure but not decisive. Negative result: no double-negation advantage and diffuse (chance-level) localization - negation is encoded into content, not as a separable additive flag.

Experiment 3 (H2 - A locatable live-polarity representation that degrades under load): Tests that each proposition's live polarity is decodable mid-chain, that decodability degrades as load rises, and that low decodability predicts drops. Data/protocol: hidden states at each proposition-mention position (after the polarity cue) across the battery; per-layer L2-regularized linear probe (3 seeds, 70/30 item-disjoint split) decoding negated-vs-affirmed live polarity; a difference-in-means polarity direction from content-matched negated/affirmed contrasts; same five frozen models. Double-negation items test that the probe reads live polarity, not surface 'not'. Decisive metric: held-out per-layer AUROC for live polarity (chance 0.5), and its degradation slope with negation_count. Convincing result: best-layer AUROC >=0.80 including on double-negation items (so it is live polarity, not surface tokens), decodability degrades significantly with negation_count (slope CI excluding 0), and low mid-chain decodability predicts final polarity-drop errors (rho >=0.30, CI excluding 0) - and this degradation mediates the negation_count->error effect. Indecision band: AUROC 0.65-0.80, or a prediction rho 0.15-0.30 - a polarity representation exists but its load-degradation link to errors is tentative. Negative result: AUROC <0.65 or no degradation-to-error link - no separable, load-sensitive polarity representation.

Experiment 4 (H3 - The load is causally relievable by steering and patching): Tests that restoring the polarity representation rescues dropped negations and that suppressing it induces drops. Data/protocol: (a) activation patching - on trials heading toward a polarity drop, cache the correct polarity representation of the relevant proposition from an early position and patch it into the pre-drop position; specificity via cross-proposition and random-matched-vector patches. (b) steering - amplify (+) the polarity direction for the relevant proposition under high load and suppress (-) it at low load, 4 coefficients; controls random-direction and no-steer; same five frozen models; specificity tracked on zero-negation items and fluency. Decisive metric: polarity-drop rescue rate under patching (versus cross-proposition/random), and change in accuracy/drop-rate under steering. Convincing result: correct-polarity patching rescues >=30% of pre-drop trials while cross-proposition/random patches rescue <10% (so it is the polarity, not leaked answer content), +polarity steering reduces drops by >=5 pp under high load with monotonic dose-response, -polarity steering induces drops at low load, and zero-negation accuracy and fluency are preserved. Indecision band: rescue 10-30%, or a 2-5 pp steering effect - a causal contribution present but not clean. Negative result: rescue <=random, or <2 pp steering effect - polarity is not a causally load-bearing, separable quantity.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 - High-stakes clinical instance): Tests that stacking negated findings drives silent decision-flipping drops and that steering/patching reduces them. Data: ~250 clinical vignettes containing a variable count of negated findings ('no history of X', 'not on anticoagulants', 'contraindicated'), each with a labeled correct diagnostic/treatment decision and a polarity-drop-induced flip; adapted from MedQA/MedMCQA stems. Protocol: same five frozen models; vary negated-finding count; compare no-steer against polarity steering/patching on fine-distinction cases; aggregate reporting only. Decisive metric: silent decision-flip rate as a function of negated-finding count, and its reduction under intervention. Convincing result: flip rate rises with negated-finding count (slope CI excluding 0) and polarity steering/patching cuts flips on fine-distinction cases by >=6 pp versus no-steer, without harming zero-negation matched cases. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp reduction - safety-relevant but modest. Negative result: no count-dependent flip rise, or <2 pp reduction - the polarity load does not manifest as a controllable clinical hazard, bounding its practical reach.


Rival-hypothesis controls and analysis: beyond the equal-length surface-modifier control, we include marker-free logically-equivalent reformulations (separating representational additivity from surface 'not'-familiarity), balance answer frequency, and verify that patching cannot leak answer content (single-proposition polarity patches with cross-proposition/random specificity checks). The mediation test requires that mid-chain polarity-decodability degradation temporally PRECEDES the drop error rather than merely co-occurring. Sample sizes, model comparisons, and effect-size thresholds are pre-registered with 95% CIs rather than treated as arbitrary cutoffs, and the item templates plus the two-annotator meaning-preservation protocol (target >=90% agreement) are documented in the released benchmark.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) The negation-count effect could reflect general difficulty rather than a specific polarity load; mitigated by content/length/depth matching, the equal-length non-negation surface-modifier control, and the polarity-drop error signature (errors are the SPECIFIC dropped-negation answer, not random). (2) Adding negations may subtly change meaning/plausibility; we use minimal edits, verify with an entailment check and human spot-checks, and balance which propositions are negated. (3) Instruction-tuned models may handle a few negations robustly, flattening the curve at low counts; we push to higher negation counts, include harder chains, and test multiple models - a curve that only bends at high load is still informative. (4) The polarity probe may capture surface 'not' tokens rather than a maintained live-polarity representation; mitigated by probing at proposition-mention positions after the cue, held-out validation, testing on double-negation (surface has 'not' but live polarity is positive), and random-direction steering controls. (5) Patching could rescue by leaking answer content; we patch only the polarity representation of a single proposition (not the answer) and use cross-proposition/random specificity controls. (6) The polarity direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence; addressed by content-matched negated/affirmed contrasts, specificity checks on zero-negation items, and the double-negation test. (7) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (8) A null result (no compounding load, errors not polarity-shaped, no separable polarity signal) is itself informative: it would indicate LLMs encode negation into content rather than as a separable, load-bearing flag. (9) The 'polarity load / working memory' framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like working memory; clinical experiments run in controlled research settings with aggregate reporting only. (10) We treat the additive-flag claim as one of several rival representational hypotheses (additive flag vs content-entangled encoding vs uncertainty collapse vs surface-token tracking) and state which distinguishing signature each predicts, so the strongest claim is asserted only if the double-negation, marker-free, and patching-specificity tests jointly support it.

Name: acquisition_prerequisite_gating
Title: Skill Tree, Not Timeline: Does an Earlier-Acquired Linguistic Capability Causally Gate the Emergence of a Later One?
Short Hypothesis: The developmental order in which LLMs acquire linguistic capabilities (e.g., part-of-speech/morphology -> syntax -> semantic composition -> discourse) is not a mere timeline but a causal prerequisite chain: selectively delaying or degrading a model's acquisition of an earlier capability during training causally prevents or slows the emergence of the later capability that normally builds on it, even when abundant data for the later capability is present, whereas degrading a non-prerequisite (parallel) capability leaves it unaffected. We prioritize two to three well-separated, theoretically-motivated edges (morphology->syntax, syntax->semantic composition) as primary claims and treat discourse as exploratory.
Related Work: A large literature establishes that LLMs acquire linguistic structure in a consistent DEVELOPMENTAL ORDER that qualitatively mirrors children: phonemic->lexical->syntactic emergence (Emergence of Phonemic/Syntactic/Semantic Representations, 2026), POS-first (LMs Learn POS First, 2018), consistent one-dimensional grammar-learning trajectories across seeds/architectures (Grammar-Learning Trajectories, 2021), chronological probing showing discourse last (Is neural language acquisition similar to natural?, 2022), n-gram-then-refinement dynamics (N-Gram Learning, 2025), a window of maximal cognitive-developmental alignment (Development of Cognitive Intelligence in PLMs, 2024), and age-ordered curriculum effects on semantic learning (Order matters, 2018/2019). CRUCIALLY, all of this is DESCRIPTIVE and CORRELATIONAL: it characterizes WHEN capabilities emerge and in what order, but never tests whether the order reflects a CAUSAL DEPENDENCY. No prior work asks whether an earlier capability is a functional PREREQUISITE whose disruption causally blocks a later one, nor uses targeted training-data ablation to sever a specific rung of the ladder and observe downstream failure with prerequisite-vs-parallel specificity controls. We uniquely convert the observed acquisition timeline into a testable causal skill-tree via a Formation-Tracing + Causal-Intervention strategy (data-ablation re-training + checkpoint probing), distinguishing genuine prerequisite gating from co-occurrence. Novelty locus: the contribution is threefold and methodological — cross-capability causal-graph discovery (not intervention on a single construction), edge-specific rescue/reversibility, and a demonstration that the causal skill tree is strictly SPARSER than the temporal order — which is what distinguishes genuine prerequisite gating from co-occurrence. It differs from prior single-construction causal-intervention work (which perturbs one phenomenon inside an already-trained model) by manipulating acquisition itself during from-scratch training, with matched non-prerequisite and generic-slowdown baselines. Communities that would cite it include developmental and mechanistic interpretability, curriculum learning, and data curation.
Abstract: Language models acquire linguistic capabilities in a strikingly consistent developmental order that echoes child development: coarse lexical/part-of-speech knowledge first, then syntax, then semantic composition, then discourse. Existing work treats this order as a descriptive timeline. We ask a causal question: is the order a prerequisite chain? That is, does mastering an earlier capability causally enable the emergence of the later capability that builds on it, such that disrupting the earlier rung blocks the later one even when its own training signal is abundant? We test this by training small language models from scratch under controlled interventions that selectively delay or degrade the acquisition of one target capability (e.g., syntactic hierarchy) via surgical training-data ablation or curriculum manipulation, while holding total data and the later capability's signal fixed. We then probe, across training checkpoints, whether a downstream capability (e.g., semantic composition, discourse coherence) still emerges on schedule. Our central prediction is a prerequisite-specificity dissociation: disrupting a genuine prerequisite delays or prevents the downstream capability, whereas disrupting a matched non-prerequisite (parallel) capability of equal difficulty leaves the downstream capability intact. We further predict the intervention shifts the downstream capability's emergence checkpoint and lowers its ceiling in proportion to prerequisite degradation (dose-response). We characterize the resulting empirical skill tree, quantify per-edge gating strength, and test whether a late 'remedial' injection of the prerequisite can rescue the stalled downstream capability. Across several from-scratch model configurations and seeds, we convert the well-documented acquisition timeline into a causal dependency graph, revealing whether language capabilities in LLMs are a skill tree rather than a mere schedule. A simpler rival account — that any targeted degradation slows training generally or lowers data quality — is controlled by matched non-prerequisite ablations, random-token-corruption matched for signal loss, and matched perplexity/loss trajectories. If gating is confirmed, practitioners could reorder curricula, filter or augment data toward prerequisite skills, and target remediation at a blocked rung; a translational check tests whether such skill-tree-informed ordering improves sample efficiency versus standard training. If null — order is a data-statistics schedule, not a causal tree — that equally revises the developmental analogy and indicates prerequisite-targeted intervention is not worthwhile.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (Setup for H1 - Baseline acquisition order and emergence checkpoints): Establishes the reference developmental ladder and per-capability emergence checkpoints that all interventions are measured against. Data (training): a ~100M-word corpus mixing child-directed speech (the CHILDES/BabyLM strict-small 100M-word set, used as is) with Simple Wikipedia; this size is affordable for an academic lab and prior child-directed-speech work shows it suffices for the target capabilities. Data (evaluation probes, existing sets used as is): (a) lexical/POS + morphology - POS/agreement probing plus BLiMP morphology subsets (BLiMP has 67 paradigms x 1,000 pairs); (b) syntactic hierarchy - BLiMP/Zorro structural minimal pairs plus a hierarchical-generalization test on question-formation/passivization; (c) semantic composition - compositional-entailment / predicate-argument probes (adapted from existing NLI minimal pairs); (d) discourse - coreference and discourse-connective cloze. Models (trained from scratch, all weights trainable): small GPT-2-style transformers at ~10M, ~30M, ~100M parameters, depth-varied, 3-5 seeds each (seeds 0-4); dense checkpointing every ~2M tokens. Decisive metric: the ordered sequence of per-capability emergence checkpoints (first checkpoint where a probe reliably exceeds its chance/threshold band) and its cross-seed consistency (Kendall's tau across seeds). Convincing result: baselines reproduce the standard order (POS/morphology -> syntax -> composition -> discourse) with cross-seed rank consistency tau >=0.8, giving well-separated emergence checkpoints to serve as the causal baseline. Indecision band: tau 0.5-0.8 or overlapping (poorly separated) emergence windows for adjacent rungs - order is noisy and later causal edges on those rungs will be underpowered; we add seeds and denser checkpoints. Negative result (for setup): tau <0.5 or no stable order - the developmental ladder is not reliably present at this scale, so the causal test is deferred to the well-separated rungs only (POS/morphology -> syntax -> basic composition).

Experiment 2 (H1 - Severing a prerequisite blocks the downstream capability): Tests the core causal claim that degrading an earlier capability's learnable signal delays or lowers a later capability that builds on it, even with the later capability's own signal preserved. Data (training, constructed by ablation): matched corpora that selectively DEGRADE one target capability while preserving others and total token count - e.g., to degrade syntactic hierarchy, apply clause-local word-order scrambling that destroys hierarchical cues but preserves lexical co-occurrence and morphology; to degrade morphology, lemmatize/strip inflection; to degrade discourse, shuffle sentence order across documents. Each ablation passes a manipulation check (its target probe drops) while the downstream capability's own input cues are verified intact via probes. Models/protocol: retrain the same from-scratch transformers (all weights trainable, 3-5 seeds) on each single-capability-degraded corpus; probe every ~2M tokens. Decisive metric: the downstream capability's emergence-checkpoint shift and asymptotic ceiling versus baseline, modeled as downstream_probe ~ intervention*checkpoint + (1|seed). Convincing result: degrading a genuine prerequisite (e.g., syntax) delays the downstream capability's (e.g., composition) emergence checkpoint by >=25% of its baseline emergence step (CI across seeds excluding 0) AND lowers its asymptotic ceiling by >=5 pp probe accuracy, beyond what its preserved own-signal predicts. Indecision band: a 10-25% checkpoint delay or a 2-5 pp ceiling drop - a directional block that is not decisive. Negative result: <10% delay and <2 pp ceiling drop - degrading the prerequisite does not gate the downstream capability, evidence that the acquisition order is a data-statistics schedule, not a causal skill tree.

Experiment 3 (H1 - Prerequisite-vs-parallel specificity dissociation): The key control ruling out generic training disruption or lost tokens. Data (training, constructed): degrade a matched NON-PREREQUISITE / parallel capability of comparable probe difficulty and token footprint, plus a random-token-corruption corpus matched for total signal loss. Models/protocol: as Experiment 2, same seeds. Decisive metric: the downstream capability's checkpoint/ceiling change under the parallel-capability (and random-corruption) ablation, contrasted with the prerequisite ablation. Convincing result: the downstream capability is spared under the parallel-capability and random-corruption ablations (checkpoint shift <10% and ceiling drop <2 pp), while the prerequisite ablation from Experiment 2 shows the full effect - a clean prerequisite-specific dissociation. Indecision band: the parallel/random ablations cause a partial downstream effect (10-25% of the prerequisite effect) - the block is only partly prerequisite-specific. Negative result: parallel-capability and random-corruption ablations harm the downstream capability as much as the prerequisite ablation - the effect is generic disruption / lost signal, not prerequisite gating.

Experiment 4 (H1 - Dose-response): Tests that downstream disruption scales with how much the prerequisite is degraded. Data (training, constructed): graded degradation of the prerequisite (25/50/75/100% of its cues scrambled), total tokens fixed. Models/protocol: as above, same seeds. Decisive metric: the monotonic relation between prerequisite-degradation level and downstream emergence-delay / ceiling-drop (slope across the four levels). Convincing result: emergence-delay and ceiling-drop increase monotonically with degradation level (slope CI excluding 0), strengthening the causal reading. Indecision band: a non-monotonic or shallow trend (slope CI grazing 0) - dosage relation unclear. Negative result: no dose-response (flat across levels) - the block, if any, is threshold-like or artifactual rather than a graded prerequisite dependency.

Experiment 5 (H1 - Remedial rescue / reversibility): Tests whether restoring the prerequisite signal later lets the stalled downstream capability emerge, quantifying reversibility. Data/protocol: train under prerequisite degradation up to a fixed checkpoint, then switch to clean data restoring the prerequisite; continue probing; same models/seeds. Decisive metric: whether the downstream capability emerges after the switch, and its delay relative to baseline emergence. Convincing result: the downstream capability emerges after the prerequisite is restored (probe crosses threshold) but delayed by a measurable margin versus baseline (CI excluding 0) - the block is real but reversible once the prerequisite is supplied. Indecision band: partial recovery (downstream reaches an intermediate ceiling that neither matches baseline nor stays blocked) - reversibility is incomplete/ambiguous. Negative result: no post-switch emergence within the remaining budget - either the block is irreversible (a strong prerequisite claim) or the earlier delay was not prerequisite-driven; interpreted jointly with Experiments 2-3.

Experiment 6 (H1 - Skill-tree construction and per-edge gating strength): Aggregates the interventions into an empirical causal dependency graph and compares it to the correlational timeline.
