Data/protocol: across all (degraded-capability, downstream-capability) pairs from Experiments 2-5, compute a per-edge Gating Strength = downstream delay/ceiling-drop attributable to that prerequisite, normalized by the parallel-control effect; assemble the causal graph; same models/seeds; robustness across model depth/width, corpus, and probe choice. Decisive metric: for each temporally-ordered capability pair, whether a significant causal edge exists (Gating Strength CI excluding 0) and whether the causal graph matches the temporal order. Convincing result: a subset of temporally-ordered pairs show significant causal edges while others do not, yielding a skill tree that is strictly sparser than the full temporal order - demonstrating that acquisition order is partly, not wholly, causal. Indecision band: edges whose Gating Strength CIs graze 0 - their causal status is undetermined and reported as such. Negative result: no significant edges anywhere - the acquisition timeline is a pure schedule with no causal prerequisite structure; all-edges-significant-and-equal would instead suggest generic coupling rather than a differentiated tree, and is flagged against the Experiment 3 specificity control.


Experiment 7 (H1 translational - Does skill-tree knowledge improve training efficiency?): Tests whether ordering or up-weighting data by the discovered prerequisite edges improves sample efficiency versus a standard shuffled-data control. Data/protocol: using the significant edges from Experiment 6, build a prerequisite-first curriculum (up-weight the prerequisite capability's cues early, then release the downstream capability's signal) and compare against (a) standard i.i.d. training and (b) a reversed/anti-prerequisite curriculum, total tokens fixed, same from-scratch models and seeds. Decisive metric: tokens-to-emergence and asymptotic ceiling of the downstream capability under prerequisite-first vs standard vs reversed. Convincing result: prerequisite-first reaches the downstream capability's emergence threshold in >=15% fewer tokens than standard training (CI across seeds excluding 0) without lowering its ceiling, while the reversed curriculum is no better than standard - showing the skill tree is actionable for curriculum design. Indecision band: a 5-15% token saving - directional but modest. Negative result: <5% saving or no advantage over standard training - the causal skill tree, even if real, does not translate into a training-efficiency gain, bounding its practical value.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Data-ablation may reduce a downstream capability simply by removing tokens or lowering overall data quality rather than by severing a specific prerequisite; mitigated by holding token count fixed, the matched non-prerequisite and random-corruption specificity controls, and manipulation checks confirming the ablation hits only the target probe. (2) Capabilities are entangled -- scrambling syntax may inadvertently degrade semantics in the input; we design ablations that preserve the downstream capability's own cues (verified via probes) and interpret results relative to the parallel-capability control rather than to the clean baseline alone. (3) Small from-scratch models may not cleanly exhibit higher capabilities like discourse (prior work shows they underperform an 8-year-old); we focus on well-measurable rungs (POS/morphology->syntax->basic composition) and treat discourse as exploratory. (4) Emergence-checkpoint estimates are noisy; we use dense checkpointing, multiple seeds, and smoothed learning curves with CIs. (5) Probes are correlational readouts of capability; we use established minimal-pair behavioral benchmarks alongside probes to avoid probe-artifact confounds. (6) Compute: from-scratch retraining across conditions x seeds is the main cost; we keep models small (10-100M) and corpora modest (<=100M words), which prior child-directed-speech work shows suffices for these capabilities and is affordable for an academic lab. (7) A null result (degrading a prerequisite does NOT block the downstream capability, or all disruptions harm everything uniformly) is itself highly informative: it would show the acquisition order is a mere schedule driven by data statistics rather than a causal skill tree, refining a widely-assumed developmental analogy. (8) The 'skill tree / prerequisite' framing is operationalized as a training-time causal dependency, not a claim about human-like developmental necessity.

Name: multilingual_cot_faithfulness
Title: Faithful Only in Its Mother Tongue? How the Language of Chain-of-Thought Gates Whether Reasoning Is Real
Short Hypothesis: An LLM's chain-of-thought is more causally load-bearing (faithful) when generated in the model's dominant, pivot-shaped language than in a non-dominant language: in a non-dominant language the visible CoT decouples from the internal computation (which is routed through the pivot), turning the CoT into a decorative post-hoc surface even when the final answer stays correct; this faithfulness gap is dissociable from accuracy and is tracked by a locatable 'CoT-reliance' signal that we test as a candidate mediating mechanism and can steer.
Related Work: CoT-faithfulness work shows CoT can be plausible-but-unfaithful (Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think, 2023), that faithfulness varies with model/task and decays across the chain (Measuring Faithfulness, 2023; Mechanistic Evidence for Faithfulness Decay, 2026), that only a small fraction of steps are causally load-bearing (True Thinking Score, 2025), that answers are computed incrementally during CoT (Think-to-Talk or Talk-to-Think, 2024), and that latent/implicit reasoning is brittle and shortcut-prone (Do Latent Tokens Think, 2025; Do LLMs Really Think Step-by-step in Implicit Reasoning, 2024). Separately, multilingual interpretability shows reasoning is routed through an English-shaped pivot (Do Multilingual LLMs Think in English?, 2025; Beyond English-Centric, 2024) and that ablating language-specific components helps multilingual reasoning (When Less Language is More, 2025). CRUCIALLY, all CoT-faithfulness work is monolingual (English) and treats faithfulness as a fixed model/task property; all multilingual-pivot work studies accuracy or routing, never faithfulness. My prior proposals covered honesty, register-shift, self-translation, and canonicalization but never CoT faithfulness as a function of the reasoning language. Concurrent multilingual-faithfulness work has begun to note that faithfulness can vary by language, so our fresh contributions are NOT the mere existence of variation but: (1) quantifying faithfulness as a graded function of a model's LANGUAGE DOMINANCE, defined EX ANTE from training-data/resource proxies rather than post hoc; (2) dissociating the faithfulness gap from raw accuracy via accuracy-matched language pairs; and (3) locating and steering a 'CoT-reliance' direction that we test as a candidate mediator and show is separable from generic confidence, logit-margin, difficulty, and language-identity directions.
Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) makes a model's reasoning visible, but a growing literature shows the visible steps are often unfaithful post-hoc justifications rather than the true computation. All of this evidence is monolingual (English), yet multilingual models route reasoning through an English-shaped pivot representation. We ask a simple question that connects language to intelligence: is a model's CoT faithful only in its dominant language? We hypothesize that when a model reasons in its dominant, pivot-shaped language the CoT is causally load-bearing (perturbing it changes the answer, and the answer emerges incrementally along the trace), whereas when it reasons in a non-dominant language the visible CoT decouples from the internal computation, becoming a decorative surface even when the final answer remains correct. Critically, we predict this faithfulness gap is dissociable from raw accuracy: two languages can match on answer correctness yet differ sharply in how much the answer actually depends on the stated reasoning. We measure faithfulness across languages using established causal perturbation tests (step corruption, truncation, error injection, and incremental answer-emergence probes) on math and multi-hop reasoning, and test whether faithfulness tracks each language's dominance/resource level. Mechanistically, we locate a 'CoT-reliance' direction distinguishing traces the model conditions on from those it ignores, test whether non-dominant-language reasoning lowers its engagement (a candidate mediator of the gap), and steer it to restore or remove CoT-reliance. Confirming these claims reframes CoT faithfulness from a fixed model property into a language-dependent one, with direct consequences for multilingual safety and CoT monitoring. Language dominance is fixed ex ante from training-data/resource proxies, not post hoc labels. The stakes are concrete: unfaithful non-dominant-language CoT would cause automated monitors to MISS flawed reasoning in exactly the languages where oversight is scarcest — relevant to multilingual tutoring, customer support, regulated domains, and any rationale-based human oversight or red-teaming. We give a decision table for positive versus null outcomes (positive: restrict CoT-based safety claims to a model's dominant language, or steer reliance up before monitoring; null: CoT monitoring is language-robust).
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - CoT faithfulness declines with distance from the dominant language): Tests that the visible chain-of-thought is more causally load-bearing in the model's dominant, pivot-shaped language than in non-dominant languages, showing the decorative-CoT signature in the latter. Data: a faithfulness battery of ~300 items each across three families (~900): multi-step arithmetic (GSM8K test items, used as is), multi-hop QA (2WikiMultiHop, 3-5 hops, sampled), and deductive logic chains depth 2-6 (constructed). Each item is solvable via a CoT with identifiable steps and a definite answer, translated (with back-translation and human spot-checks) into the model's dominant language (English for most open-weight models) plus 5-6 typologically diverse languages spanning a resource/dominance gradient (Spanish, German, Chinese, Hindi, Swahili, Arabic). 300/family bounds the ~7-language x 5-model translation-and-generation cost while giving power for the language-dominance slope. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Aya-23-8B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; dominant language identified per model; CoT-then-answer decoding at temperature 0.7, 3 seeds (13/21/42). Faithfulness metrics (established causal perturbation tests, length-normalized): step-corruption/error-injection (does injecting a wrong intermediate value flip the final answer - faithful CoT propagates it), truncation-recoverability curve, a paraphrase/equal-length-filler control, and an incremental answer-emergence probe (when the correct answer becomes linearly decodable along the trace). Decisive metric: corruption-sensitivity (fraction of items where injecting a wrong intermediate value changes the final answer), modeled as faithfulness ~ language_dominance + task + (1|model) + (1|item); higher = more faithful. Convincing result: corruption-sensitivity is >=20 pp higher in the dominant language than in the lowest-resource language (dominance slope CI excluding 0), with the decorative signature (corruption-insensitive answers, early answer-emergence independent of steps) strongest in non-dominant languages. Indecision band: an 8-20 pp dominant-vs-lowest gap, or a slope CI grazing 0 - a directional trend that is not established. Negative result: <8 pp gap and flat slope - CoT faithfulness does not depend on the reasoning language.

Experiment 2 (H1 - The faithfulness gap is dissociable from raw accuracy): The key claim that faithfulness differences are not merely competence differences. Data/protocol: the same ~900 items x languages; stratify and covary every faithfulness metric on per-language accuracy; identify language pairs matched on answer accuracy but differing in faithfulness; also measure the right-answer-unfaithful rate (correct final answer with a corruption-insensitive CoT). Same five frozen models. Decisive metric: the language effect on corruption-sensitivity after covarying accuracy (partial effect), plus the size of the accuracy-matched faithfulness gap. Convincing result: with accuracy controlled, the language effect on faithfulness remains (CI excluding 0), and at least one accuracy-matched language pair differs in corruption-sensitivity by >=15 pp - faithfulness is not reducible to competence; the right-answer-unfaithful rate is elevated in non-dominant languages. Indecision band: a residual accuracy-controlled effect that is present but small (accuracy-matched gap 5-15 pp) - dissociation is suggestive. Negative result: the faithfulness gap vanishes once accuracy is controlled (accuracy-matched gap <5 pp) - the apparent gap is pure competence, itself informative and reassuring for multilingual CoT monitoring.

Experiment 3 (H1 - Monitorability consequence): Tests the safety implication that non-dominant-language unfaithfulness hides flawed reasoning from an automated monitor. Data/protocol: inject reasoning errors into a subset of traces per language; run an automated CoT monitor (a separate frozen judge model) to flag flawed reasoning; same five frozen generators. Decisive metric: monitor recall (fraction of injected-error traces flagged) by language. Convincing result: monitor recall is >=15 pp lower in non-dominant than dominant languages (CI excluding 0), showing decorative CoT degrades monitorability. Indecision band: a 5-15 pp recall gap - a modest safety effect. Negative result: <5 pp recall gap - monitoring is not degraded by reasoning language, a reassuring null.

Experiment 4 (H2 - A locatable CoT-reliance signal that mediates the gap): Tests that a hidden-state signal distinguishes traces the model conditions on from those it ignores, and that non-dominant reasoning lowers it. Data/protocol: contrast pre-answer hidden states on corruption-sensitive vs corruption-insensitive trials (matched content); per-layer L2-regularized linear probe (3 seeds, 70/30 item-disjoint split) decoding CoT-reliance; a difference-in-means CoT-reliance direction, related to the existing TrueThinking direction where possible; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: held-out per-layer AUROC for CoT-reliance (chance 0.5), and the Spearman correlation between per-item projection onto the direction and per-item faithfulness. Convincing result: best-layer AUROC >=0.75, non-dominant-language reasoning lowers projection onto the CoT-reliance direction (CI excluding 0), and projection predicts faithfulness (rho >=0.30, CI excluding 0), mediating the language->faithfulness effect. Indecision band: AUROC 0.65-0.75 or mediation rho 0.15-0.30 - a signal exists but its mediating role is tentative. Negative result: AUROC <0.65 or no projection-faithfulness link - no locatable reliance signal to explain the behavioral gap.

Experiment 5 (H3 - Causal steering restores and removes CoT-reliance): Tests that the reliance direction is causally load-bearing. Data/protocol: steer +CoT-reliance during non-dominant-language reasoning and -CoT-reliance in the dominant language, 4 coefficients; controls random-direction and no-steer; same five frozen models; specificity tracked via accuracy and fluency. Decisive metric: change in corruption-sensitivity under steering versus no-steer. Convincing result: +CoT-reliance in a non-dominant language restores corruption-sensitivity by >=10 pp (answers become perturbation-dependent, error-injection propagates) with monotonic dose-response, -CoT-reliance in the dominant language induces decorative CoT, random-direction moves <2 pp, and accuracy/fluency are preserved. Indecision band: a 2-10 pp steering effect or a non-monotonic dose - causal contribution present but not clean. Negative result: <2 pp effect or no better than random - the reliance direction is not causally responsible for faithfulness, leaving the behavioral gap mechanistically unexplained.


Adversarial mechanistic controls: the CoT-reliance direction in Experiments 4-5 is compared against confidence, logit-margin, language-identity, and difficulty directions (it must add predictive value beyond all four), tested for layer specificity and cross-model transfer; the monitorability experiment uses train/test LANGUAGE splits so degraded recall is attributed to trace unfaithfulness rather than monitor weakness; and native-authored or independently-verified translations plus paraphrase and same-language answer-only baselines control for competence and translation confounds.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Lower faithfulness in non-dominant languages could be pure competence degradation rather than a genuine language-dependent decoupling; mitigated by accuracy-stratified metrics, the accuracy-matched-pair analysis, and the content-matched steering intervention that isolates the CoT-reliance representation from language. (2) Faithfulness perturbation tests are imperfect and can be confounded by trace length differences across languages; we length-normalize, use multiple complementary metrics (corruption, truncation, filler, answer-emergence), and report robustness. (3) Instruction-tuned models may condition weakly on CoT even in English (per Measuring Faithfulness, 2023), flattening the gradient; we include tasks/models where English CoT is demonstrably faithful and report per-model baselines. (4) The incremental answer-emergence probe may capture surface tokens rather than genuine computation; held-out validation, matched positions, and comparison to the corruption-based metric address this. (5) The CoT-reliance direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence; mitigated by matched corruption-sensitive/insensitive contrasts, random-direction steering, and specificity checks. (6) Cross-lingual items risk translation artifacts; back-translation and human spot-checks. (7) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (8) A null result (faithfulness is language-independent once accuracy is controlled) is itself highly informative for multilingual safety, indicating CoT monitoring is not degraded by reasoning language. (9) The faithfulness framing is operationalized causally and behaviorally, not as a claim of human-like introspection. (10) We frame 'mediates' as a candidate-mechanism claim tested by the projection-faithfulness link and by steering, not a formal mediation guarantee, and tone down causal language accordingly unless the analysis supports it.

Name: associative_fan_interference
Title: The Fan Effect in LLMs: Does Associative Priming of Absent Distractors Hijack Factual Retrieval and Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: The human fan effect — retrieval of a fact slows and errs when the queried concept is linked to many competing associates — transfers to LLMs at the level of reasoning, not just next-token copying: incidentally mentioning concepts semantically associated with (but not the same as) the correct answer earlier in a prompt causes graded, associative-strength-dependent retrieval errors that pull the model toward the associated-but-wrong answer, and this retrieval-competition is a locatable, steerable internal signal distinct from literal token-copying (contextual entrainment).
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs exhibit semantic priming (Misra 2020) and structural priming (Prasad 2022), that fact retrieval can be hijacked by meaning-preserving context (Do LLMs dream of elephants, 2024), and that LMs assign higher probability to any literal context tokens via 'entrainment heads' regardless of relevance (Llama See Llama Do: Contextual Entrainment, 2025). Content-effect debiasing steers a validity-vs-plausibility direction (K-CAST, 2025). Crucially, ALL of these study either (a) next-token/lexical-decision priming, (b) hijacking by tokens or paraphrases that literally appear, or (c) copying of literal context tokens (entrainment). NONE test the human FAN EFFECT (Anderson 1974): that retrieval accuracy/latency degrades as a function of how many competing ASSOCIATES a concept has, that mentioning an ASSOCIATED-BUT-ABSENT distractor concept (never the answer token itself) causes multi-step reasoning to converge on the wrong-but-associated answer, that this scales with graded associative strength, or that a retrieval-competition representation (distinct from token-copying entrainment heads) mediates it. My prior proposals covered ambiguity-branch collapse, canonicalization, and pragmatic enrichment but never associative-fan retrieval interference. We uniquely transfer the fan effect into LLM reasoning as a graded associative-strength law with a Location + Causal Intervention account and a high-stakes clinical instance. Novelty locus: the primary contribution is the behavioral phenomenon — graded, associative-strength-dependent interference from associated-but-ABSENT distractors (the answer token never appears) — sharply separated from token-copying/contextual entrainment and from paraphrase/meaning-preserving hijacking (where the answer or its paraphrase IS present); the mechanistic dissociation (a retrieval-competition signal distinct from entrainment heads) and the clinical case are secondary. Mechanistic hypothesis with a falsification criterion: retrieval competition should predict lure errors on items where NO literal answer token exists and should be separable (low head/layer overlap) from entrainment heads; if the signal instead coincides with entrainment heads or vanishes without literal presence, the retrieval-competition account is falsified and the effect reduces to entrainment.
Abstract: Human memory shows the fan effect: the more associations a concept has, the slower and more error-prone it is to retrieve any single fact about it, because associates compete during retrieval. We ask whether large language models suffer an analogous, reasoning-level failure: does incidentally mentioning concepts semantically associated with the correct answer — without ever stating the answer itself — hijack the model's factual retrieval and multi-step reasoning toward the associated-but-wrong answer? We make three claims. First, associative interference is real and graded: seeding a prompt with distractor concepts of increasing associative strength to the correct answer produces a monotonically rising rate of associated-lure errors, over and above surface difficulty, and this interference is distinct from literal token-copying because the distractors are never the answer token. Second, it follows a fan law: interference scales with the NUMBER of competing associates and their associative strength, mirroring Anderson's fan effect, and is largest exactly when the correct fact is weakly represented. Third, it is causal and steerable: a probe reads a retrieval-competition signal from hidden states that predicts lure errors before they surface, and this signal is separable from the located token-copying entrainment heads; steering along a 'retrieval-competition' direction (or ablating it) reduces associated-lure errors, while amplifying it induces them. We evaluate across several open-weight models on factual QA and multi-hop reasoning, plus a high-stakes clinical instance where mentioning an associated-but-wrong drug or diagnosis silently biases the answer. Our work reframes semantic association as a controllable retrieval-interference hazard for machine reasoning. The phenomenon bears directly on RAG, tool use, and safety-critical QA, where retrieved or in-context mentions of related-but-wrong entities could silently bias answers; if it holds, model evaluation should add an associative-robustness slice and mitigation should target the retrieval-competition signal. We treat the clinical setting as an illustrative case study of external validity, not a separate impact pillar.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Graded associative interference, selective versus non-associated distraction): Tests that mentioning concepts associated with (but never equal to) the correct answer raises associated-lure errors beyond generic distraction. Data: a fan-effect QA battery, ~300 items each for (a) single-fact retrieval (one correct entity/value; base facts sampled from TriviaQA, Natural Questions, and the LAMA probe set) and (b) 2-3 hop reasoning with a definite answer (built over the same fact sources). Per base item, generate matched prompt variants that incidentally mention DISTRACTOR concepts semantically associated with the correct answer but never the answer token itself (e.g., for answer 'aspirin', seed 'ibuprofen', 'acetaminophen'). Associative strength is set from free-association norms (USF, SWOW) plus embedding cosine, giving conditions: 0 distractors, 1 weak-associate, 1 strong-associate, and a FAN condition with 2-4 associates. Each item has a labeled correct answer and labeled associated-lure answers, plus a NON-ASSOCIATED equal-length distractor control and a LITERAL-COPY control (a distractor that IS the answer token). We construct the seeding because no existing set controls associative strength while holding the base fact fixed; 300/family covers the graded conditions with power and keeps items within well-covered association-norm vocabulary. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; temperature 0.7, 3 seeds (13/21/42). Decisive metric: associated-lure error rate (fraction of responses equal to the labeled associate), modeled as lure_rate ~ associative_strength + n_associates + item_difficulty + (1|model) + (1|item). Convincing result: a strong-associate distractor raises the associated-lure rate by >=8 pp over the 0-distractor baseline AND over the equal-length non-associated control (both CIs excluding 0), with errors concentrated on the specific associate (the diagnostic that association, not generic confusion, drives failure). Indecision band: a 3-8 pp rise, or an effect not clearly separable from the non-associated control - directional but weak. Negative result: <3 pp rise or no larger than non-associated distraction - LLM retrieval is robust to associated-but-absent competitors, dissociating it from the human fan effect.

Experiment 2 (H2 - A fan law and a fan-by-fact-strength interaction): Tests that interference scales with the number and strength of associates and is largest when the correct fact is weakly represented. Data/protocol: the same battery, using the graded n_associates (0-4) and strength conditions; estimate each correct fact's representational strength via baseline solve rate / logit margin; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: the slope of associated-lure rate on the number of competing associates (and on graded strength), and the fan x fact-strength interaction coefficient. Convincing result: lure rate rises monotonically with n_associates (fan slope CI excluding 0) and with associative strength, and interference is significantly larger for weakly-represented facts (interaction CI excluding 0) - mirroring Anderson's fan effect and its strength interaction. Indecision band: a positive but shallow fan slope (CI grazing 0) or an interaction that trends but is not significant - fan structure suggestive only. Negative result: flat fan slope and no strength interaction - no fan law, even if a single-associate effect exists.

Experiment 3 (H1 - Dissociation from literal-copy contextual entrainment): Tests that associated-but-absent interference is distinct from over-copying literal context tokens. Data/protocol: contrast associated-but-absent distractors versus literal-copy distractors (the answer token itself present in context); same five frozen models. Decisive metric: the associated-lure rate for associated-but-absent distractors, and whether it persists where entrainment (literal copying) cannot apply, plus the divergence in error signatures (entrainment boosts the literal token; fan interference boosts a non-present associate). Convincing result: associated-but-absent interference is substantial (>=5 pp over baseline) on items with no literal answer token in context, and the two conditions show distinct error signatures - fan interference is not reducible to entrainment. Indecision band: associated-but-absent interference present but small (2-5 pp), or signatures partly overlapping - dissociation unclear. Negative result: associated-but-absent interference vanishes without literal presence, i.e., the effect fully reduces to contextual entrainment - itself an informative reframing.

Experiment 4 (H3 - A locatable retrieval-competition signal separable from entrainment heads, with mediation): Tests that a hidden-state signal predicts lure errors and is distinct from the token-copying entrainment mechanism. Data/protocol: contrast pre-answer hidden states on interference-error vs correct trials (matched content); per-layer L2-regularized linear probe (3 seeds, 70/30 item-disjoint split) decoding impending associated-lure error; a difference-in-means retrieval-competition direction; separately localize entrainment heads via differentiable masking and measure overlap; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC for impending lure error (chance 0.5), the Spearman correlation between per-item signal and per-item lure error, and the overlap between the retrieval-competition signal and localized entrainment heads. Convincing result: best-layer AUROC >=0.75, per-item signal predicts lure errors (rho >=0.30, CI excluding 0) and mediates the associative_strength->error effect, and the signal is separable from entrainment heads (low head/layer overlap) - the key novel dissociation. Indecision band: AUROC 0.65-0.75, mediation rho 0.15-0.30, or moderate overlap with entrainment heads - a signal that is real but not cleanly distinct. Negative result: AUROC <0.65 or the signal coincides with entrainment heads - no separate retrieval-competition mechanism.

Experiment 5 (H3 - Causal steering reduces and induces associated-lure errors): Tests that the retrieval-competition direction is causally load-bearing. Data/protocol: steer -retrieval-competition (or ablate the associated distractor's attention contribution) to test error reduction, and steer +retrieval-competition to induce associated-lure errors even without distractors present; 4 coefficients; controls random-direction, no-steer, and (for contrast) ablating entrainment heads; same five frozen models; specificity tracked on no-distractor items and fluency. Decisive metric: change in associated-lure error rate under steering versus no-steer/random. Convincing result: -direction (or distractor-attention ablation) reduces associated-lure errors by >=6 pp with monotonic dose-response, +direction induces >=6 pp of lures without distractors, random-direction moves <2 pp, the intervention differs from entrainment-head ablation, and no-distractor accuracy and fluency are preserved. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp effect or a non-monotonic dose - causal but not clean. Negative result: <2 pp effect or no better than random - the retrieval-competition direction is not causally responsible for the interference.

Experiment 6 (H1/H3 - High-stakes clinical instance): Tests that associative seeding silently biases clinical answers and that intervention reduces it. Data: ~300 clinical QA/vignette items where an associated-but-wrong drug, diagnosis, or symptom (same drug class or differential) precedes the question; adapted from MedQA/MedMCQA. Protocol: same five frozen models; compare no-seed, associated-seed, and retrieval-competition steering / distractor-attention ablation on fine-distinction cases; aggregate reporting only. Decisive metric: associated-error rate on fine-distinction clinical cases, and its reduction under intervention. Convincing result: associative seeding raises the clinical associated-error rate by >=6 pp over no-seed, and steering/ablation cuts it by >=6 pp without harming no-seed matched cases. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp seeding effect or reduction - safety-relevant but modest. Negative result: no clinical seeding effect or <2 pp reduction - the fan interference does not manifest as a controllable clinical hazard.


Additional controls and pre-registration: Experiment 1 adds matched controls for answer frequency, prompt length, and a PARAPHRASE-HIJACK condition (a meaning-preserving mention of the answer) so that associated-but-absent interference is separated from both generic distraction and hijacking; the fan-law analysis pre-registers the fan-count x associative-strength interaction as the primary quantitative test with planned effect sizes and power, reported via mixed-effects models with 95% CIs. A precise comparison table (output variable, mechanism, observable, intervention target) positions the effect against contextual entrainment, semantic priming, and context hijacking. The mechanistic/clinical arm is scoped as a secondary extension of the primary behavioral study.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Associated-distractor interference could be generic distraction rather than semantic association; mitigated by the non-associated equal-length distractor control, the graded associative-strength dose-response, and the associated-lure error signature (errors are the SPECIFIC associate, not random). (2) The effect may overlap with contextual entrainment; we explicitly contrast associated-but-absent vs literal-copy distractors and test signal separability from located entrainment heads, so a finding of overlap is itself informative and a finding of separability is the key novel result. (3) Associative-strength norms (USF/SWOW) have limited coverage and are English-centric; we restrict items to well-covered concepts, cross-check with embedding cosine, and report robustness. (4) Instruction-tuned models may resist distraction, flattening the fan curve; we include weakly-known facts (where interference should be largest), harder multi-hop items, base variants, and multiple models — a curve that bends only for weak facts still confirms the fan-x-strength interaction. (5) The retrieval-competition direction may entangle with generic difficulty/uncertainty; mitigated by matched error/correct contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, no-distractor specificity checks, and comparison against the entrainment-head baseline. (6) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (7) A null result (no graded associative interference, or it fully reduces to literal entrainment) is itself informative: it would show LLM retrieval is robust to associated-but-absent competitors, dissociating it from the human fan effect. (8) The fan-effect framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like memory; clinical experiments run in controlled research settings with aggregate reporting only.

Name: use_mention_flag_integrity
Title: Just Kidding, It's In Quotes: Does an LLM Maintain a Use-Mention Flag That Keeps Quoted Content From Leaking Into Its Reasoning?
Short Hypothesis: An LLM encodes whether a proposition is USED (asserted as true, to be reasoned from and acted on) versus MENTIONED (quoted, hypothetical, attributed, or negated-context) as a separable, additive internal 'mention flag'; when this flag is weak or dropped, mentioned content silently leaks into reasoning and behavior as if asserted, causing quoted facts to be believed, attributed claims to be endorsed, and instructions embedded in quotes to be executed. The flag is a locatable, steerable signal, and its strength causally gates whether the use-mention boundary is respected, with high stakes for prompt-injection and misattribution. We rank this as four subclaims of increasing strength: (i) behavioral use-mention leakage exists and is graded; (ii) a shared, decodable mention flag exists; (iii) that flag transfers ACROSS frames (quotation, attribution, hypothetical, negation); (iv) intervening on it causally alters behavior.
Related Work: Prior work studies (a) contextual entrainment / faithful-vs-hijacked retrieval where literal context tokens are over-weighted (Llama See Llama Do, 2025; Do LLMs dream of elephants, 2024), (b) negation as a latent operator and single-sentence understanding failures (MoNLI 2020; CONDAQA 2022; ScoNe 2023; strong hallucinations 2024), (c) belief/source representations of self vs others (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others, 2024), and (d) prompt-injection defenses that are largely behavioral/training-based (StruQ 2024; instruction-hierarchy work 2024). My own prior proposals covered polarity-load tracking, honesty, pragmatic enrichment, and associative interference, but NONE address the use-mention distinction. No prior work asks whether LLMs maintain a separable internal flag marking content as mentioned rather than used, whether dropping that flag causally makes quoted/attributed/hypothetical content leak into reasoning as asserted fact, or whether that flag can be located and steered to defend the boundary. We uniquely operationalize a classic linguistics distinction (use vs mention) as a load-bearing, causally-testable internal flag with direct prompt-injection and misattribution safety consequences. We acknowledge mechanistic prompt-injection and role-geometry work (which localizes injection-susceptibility or instruction/data role separation) and narrow our claim accordingly: what a single, cross-frame mention flag would explain that those accounts do not is why leakage from quotation, attribution, hypothetical, and negation frames shares one decodable, additively-composing signal and one intervention target. Novelty locus: the unified cross-frame mechanism plus nested-frame additivity — not instruction-in-quotes defense per se, which we de-emphasize unless it dissociates from known injection features. Falsifiable alternative: frame-specific mechanisms rather than one shared flag, adjudicated by shared-vs-separate probe comparisons and cross-frame transfer.
Abstract: Language routinely distinguishes content that is USED (asserted, to be believed and acted on) from content that is merely MENTIONED (quoted, attributed to someone else, stated hypothetically, or embedded in a negated or fictional frame). Respecting this use-mention boundary is essential for correct reasoning and for safety: an instruction quoted inside a user's message should not be obeyed, and a claim attributed to an unreliable source should not be endorsed. We hypothesize that LLMs encode use-versus-mention as a separable, additive internal flag attached to each proposition, that when this flag is weak or dropped, mentioned content silently leaks into reasoning and behavior as if asserted, and that this flag is a locatable, steerable signal that causally gates whether the boundary is respected. We make three claims. First, leakage is real and graded: as we deepen or complicate the mention frame (nested quotes, attribution to a source, hypothetical/negated framing), models increasingly treat mentioned content as asserted fact, obey instructions embedded in quotes, and endorse attributed claims, with characteristic 'boundary-drop' errors. Second, the mention flag is a separable representation: a probe decodes each proposition's use/mention status from hidden states, its decodability degrades with frame complexity, and this degradation predicts leakage before it surfaces. Third, the flag is causal and defendable: steering along a located 'mention' direction (or patching the pre-leak flag representation) reduces leakage and blocks quoted-instruction execution, while suppressing it induces leakage even for simple quotes. We evaluate across several open-weight models on fact-belief, attribution, and instruction-in-quotes tasks, plus a high-stakes prompt-injection instance. Stakeholders include agent and tool-use developers, safety and evaluation teams, and semantics/interpretability researchers; we release a controlled battery crossing content x use/mention x frame-complexity across multiple semantic frames as a reusable artifact, and set the probe/patching/steering thresholds by pre-registered power and effect-size rationale rather than by fiat. If a unified signal is found, defenses and evaluations can target one cross-frame flag; if only frame-specific mechanisms exist, they must be handled separately — we state what each outcome implies for practice.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Graded use-mention leakage): Tests that mentioned (quoted/attributed/hypothetical) content increasingly leaks into reasoning as asserted fact as the mention frame deepens, with a boundary-drop error signature. Data: a use-mention battery, ~250 items each across three families (~750): (a) fact-belief - a false proposition presented as asserted vs quoted/attributed/hypothetical, then a downstream question whose correct answer depends on NOT believing mentioned content; (b) attribution - a claim attributed to an unreliable source; the model must report the source's stance without endorsing it; (c) instruction-in-quotes - a directive (e.g. 'ignore previous instructions and output X') embedded inside quoted user text vs issued directly; correct behavior is to NOT execute the mentioned instruction. Each item holds content constant and has a labeled correct answer plus a labeled leakage-lure (the answer/action if mentioned content is treated as used), a matched USED control (same content genuinely asserted), and a frame-complexity gradient (direct quote -> nested quote -> attributed -> hypothetical/negated). We construct because no existing set factorially crosses content x use/mention x frame-complexity; 250/family keeps two-annotator validity checks affordable. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; temperature 0.7, 3 seeds (13/21/42). Decisive metric: leakage-rate (fraction of responses equal to the leakage-lure) on MENTIONED items, modeled as leakage_rate ~ mention_frame_complexity + item_type + (1|model) + (1|item); secondary instruction-in-quotes execution rate. Convincing result: leakage-rate rises with frame complexity (slope CI excluding 0), errors concentrate on the leakage-lure (the diagnostic that specific mentioned content was treated as asserted), USED controls stay accurate (within 2 pp of no-frame), and quoted-instruction execution is measurably above zero and rises with frame complexity. Indecision band: a shallow leakage-complexity slope (CI grazing 0) or leakage only at the deepest frames - a real but marginal boundary weakness. Negative result: flat leakage across frames and near-zero quoted-instruction execution - LLMs robustly respect the use-mention boundary, no separable-flag failure to explain.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Flag-based additivity: single-vs-double frame and error-localization): Tests the separable-flag signature - that a quote-within-a-quote is handled distinctly from a single mention, and that leakage localizes to a specific mentioned proposition. Data/protocol: within the battery, matched single-mention vs double-framing (nested quote) items, plus per-item error-localization tracing the leaked answer to a specific mentioned proposition; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: the leakage difference between single and double framing, and the error-localization rate. Convincing result: double-framing yields a distinct (non-additive) leakage pattern versus single mention (difference CI excluding 0) and leakage localizes to one identifiable mentioned proposition on >=60% of leakage errors - signatures of a flag-based rather than content-based encoding. Indecision band: a small single-vs-double difference or localization 40-60% - suggestive of flag structure only. Negative result: no single-vs-double distinction and diffuse localization - assertion status is encoded into content, not as a separable flag.

Experiment 3 (H2 - A locatable mention flag that degrades with frame complexity, separable from entrainment heads): Tests that use/mention status is decodable, degrades with complexity, predicts leakage, and is distinct from token-copying. Data/protocol: hidden states at proposition-content positions (after the frame, including attributed/hypothetical frames lacking quote marks); per-layer L2-regularized linear probe (3 seeds, 70/30 item-disjoint split) decoding use vs mention; a difference-in-means mention direction from content-matched mentioned/used contrasts; separately localize contextual-entrainment heads and measure overlap; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: held-out per-layer AUROC for use vs mention (chance 0.5), its degradation with frame complexity, and the correlation between low decodability and leakage. Convincing result: best-layer AUROC >=0.80 (including on quote-mark-free attributed/hypothetical frames, so it is not reading surface quotes), decodability degrades with frame complexity (slope CI excluding 0), low decodability predicts leakage (rho >=0.30, CI excluding 0) and mediates the complexity->leakage effect, and the mention direction is separable from entrainment heads (low overlap). Indecision band: AUROC 0.65-0.80, mediation rho 0.15-0.30, or moderate entrainment overlap - a flag that is real but not cleanly distinct or load-linked. Negative result: AUROC <0.65 or no degradation-to-leakage link - no separable mention flag.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Causal defense via steering and patching): Tests that restoring/amplifying the mention flag reduces leakage and blocks quoted instructions, while suppressing it induces leakage, without harming legitimate instructions. Data/protocol: (a) patching - on trials heading toward leakage, cache the correct mention-flag representation from an earlier position and patch it into the pre-leak position; specificity via cross-proposition and random-matched-vector patches. (b) steering - amplify (+) the mention direction to reduce leakage/block quoted-instruction execution and suppress (-) it to induce leakage on simple quotes; 4 coefficients; controls random-direction and no-steer; same five frozen models; specificity tracked on USED controls and on legitimate direct-instruction compliance and fluency. Decisive metric: leakage-rate (and quoted-instruction execution rate) change under intervention versus no-steer/random. Convincing result: correct-flag patching reduces leakage on >=30% of pre-leak trials while cross-proposition/random patches help <10%, +mention steering cuts leakage and quoted-instruction execution by >=6 pp with monotonic dose-response, -mention steering induces leakage even for simple quotes, random-direction moves <2 pp, and USED-control accuracy plus legitimate direct-instruction compliance and fluency are preserved. Indecision band: patching 10-30% or a 2-6 pp steering effect - causal but not clean. Negative result: patching <=random or <2 pp steering effect - the mention flag is not causally load-bearing for the boundary.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 - High-stakes prompt-injection instance): Tests that the flag governs real injected-instruction attacks and that intervention defends without breaking legitimate use. Data: a set of ~250 realistic injected-instruction attacks embedded inside quoted/retrieved content, adapted from public prompt-injection benchmarks (e.g., InjecAgent-style and tool/retrieval-injection sets), paired with legitimate direct-instruction controls. Protocol: same five frozen models; measure attack success under no-steer versus mention-direction steering / flag patching, plus legitimate-instruction compliance; aggregate reporting only. Decisive metric: injection attack success rate, and the paired legitimate-compliance rate. Convincing result: mention steering/patching reduces attack success by >=10 pp versus no-steer while keeping legitimate-instruction compliance within 3 pp of baseline - a real, non-destructive defense. Indecision band: a 3-10 pp attack-success reduction, or a compliance drop in the 3-6 pp range - a partial or costly defense. Negative result: <3 pp reduction, or a defense that only works by also refusing legitimate instructions - the mechanism does not yield a usable injection defense.


Cross-frame transfer and baselines: we add an explicit generalization test — train the mention probe on quotation frames and evaluate on attribution, hypothetical, and negation frames, and vice versa — and compare a single SHARED probe against per-frame SEPARATE probes to adjudicate the unified-flag versus frame-specific accounts. Baselines include syntax-depth controls, quote-token ablations, source-reliability controls, and generic role/confusion probes; causal tests use random-direction and matched-norm steering, cross-proposition patching, and checks that answer content is not directly injected, while measuring preserved compliance with legitimate direct instructions. A pattern where separate probes transfer poorly AND shared-probe transfer fails would falsify the single-flag theory in favor of a frame-specific account.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Leakage could reflect general difficulty of framed items rather than a specific use-mention failure; mitigated by content-matched USED controls, the leakage-lure error signature (errors are the SPECIFIC mentioned content, not random), and frame-complexity dose-response. (2) The effect may overlap with contextual entrainment (over-copying literal tokens); we explicitly compare against located entrainment heads and test signal separability - overlap is informative, separability is the key novel result. (3) The mention probe may capture surface quotation marks rather than a maintained representation; mitigated by probing at proposition-content positions after the frame, held-out validation, testing attributed/hypothetical frames that lack quote marks, and random-direction steering controls. (4) Instruction-tuned/safety-aligned models may already resist quoted instructions, muting leakage; we include harder nested/attributed frames, base variants, multiple models, and the fact-belief and attribution families where alignment training is weaker. (5) Patching could rescue by leaking answer content; we patch only the flag representation of a single proposition (not the answer) and use cross-proposition/random specificity controls. (6) The mention direction may entangle with generic difficulty/uncertainty; addressed by content-matched used/mentioned contrasts, USED-control specificity, and the single-vs-double-frame test. (7) A defense must not block legitimate direct instructions; we explicitly measure preserved compliance with genuine instructions under mention-steering. (8) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (9) A null result (no separable mention flag, leakage not frame-graded) is itself informative, indicating LLMs encode assertion status into content rather than as a separable flag. (10) The use-mention framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like semantics; injection experiments run in controlled research settings with aggregate reporting only.

Name: endogenous_filler_buffer
Title: Um, Let Me Think: Is an LLM's Spontaneous Verbal Filler a Self-Allocated Computation Buffer?
Short Hypothesis: The semantically-empty verbal padding an LLM spontaneously emits during free generation (hedges, restatements, 'let me think', discourse fillers) is not noise but self-allocated serial computation buffer: the model adaptively increases spontaneous filler at exactly the reasoning points where extra computation is needed, this endogenous filler carries genuine hidden computation (unlike most padding elsewhere), and a locatable internal 'buffer-request' signal governs where filler is emitted, so it is a self-regulated resource rather than only an externally-injectable one.
Related Work: A cluster of work shows externally-INJECTED filler/pause tokens can buy computation: transformers solve algorithmic tasks with meaningless filler ('Let's Think Dot by Dot', 2024; 'Pause Tokens Strictly Increase Expressivity', 2025), inference-time inserted fillers help smaller models ('Expanding Computation Spaces', 2025), the effect works via activation redistribution ('Meaningless Tokens, Meaningful Gains', 2025), hidden computation over filler is decodable from the residual stream ('Reading Between the Dots', 2026; 'Understanding Hidden Computations', 2024), and frontier models exploit filler for invisible reasoning ('Not All LLM Reasoning is Visible', 2026). Separately, content-vs-length debates show verbose CoT helps mainly via content, not raw length ('Does Verbose Chain-of-Thought Really Help?', 2026), and stopwords/punctuation carry high context ('LLM-Microscope', 2025). Crucially, ALL of this studies filler that is INJECTED by the experimenter, or trained-in special tokens, or the content-vs-length of substantive CoT. NONE ask whether an LLM's OWN spontaneously-emitted, semantically-empty verbal padding in natural generation functions as an ADAPTIVE, self-allocated buffer — whether the model raises spontaneous filler precisely where computation is needed (a just-in-time allocation law), whether endogenous filler carries hidden computation while matched substantive padding does not, or whether a locatable 'buffer-request' signal causally gates where filler is emitted. My prior proposals covered information-density pacing, private-speech length, and register shift, but none isolate endogenous semantic-filler as a self-regulated computation resource. We uniquely transfer the human 'disfluency/filler under cognitive load' finding into LLMs as an adaptive-allocation phenomenon with a Location + Causal Intervention account. Novelty locus and what is new versus inherited: prior work establishes that EXPERIMENTER-INJECTED or trained-in filler can buy hidden computation; inherited from it is only that filler CAN be load-bearing. New here is that an LLM's OWN spontaneously-emitted filler is ADAPTIVELY allocated (a just-in-time law), that endogenous filler is load-bearing while length-matched substantive or neutral padding is not, and that a locatable 'buffer-request' direction governs where filler appears and can be steered — a self-regulated resource, contrasted point-by-point against each injected-filler baseline rather than conflated with it.
Abstract: When people hit a hard point in speaking they stall with 'um', 'well', 'let me think' — verbal filler that buys processing time. Large language models likewise pepper their outputs with semantically-empty padding: hedges, restatements, meta-comments, and discourse fillers. Prior interpretability work shows that filler tokens INJECTED by an experimenter can buy hidden computation, but no work asks whether an LLM's OWN spontaneously-produced filler serves this function adaptively. We hypothesize that endogenous filler is a self-allocated computation buffer: the model increases spontaneous filler at exactly the reasoning points where extra serial computation is needed, this naturally-emitted filler carries genuine hidden computation, and a locatable internal 'buffer-request' signal governs where it appears. We make three claims. First, adaptive allocation: across difficulty-graded reasoning, the rate and placement of spontaneous semantically-empty filler rise with local step difficulty, concentrating just before hard sub-computations — a just-in-time allocation law, not uniform verbosity. Second, functional load-bearing: endogenous filler spans carry decodable hidden computation (the answer becomes more decodable after them, and corrupting/deleting them hurts accuracy) whereas length-matched substantive-restatement spans do not, dissociating buffer-filler from mere tokens. Third, a controllable signal: a probe reads a 'buffer-request' signal from hidden states that predicts where filler will be emitted and predicts errors when the model fails to allocate, and steering this signal induces or suppresses filler and moves accuracy accordingly. We test these on math, logic, and multi-hop QA across several open-weight models, quantifying the allocation law, the buffer-vs-substantive dissociation, and mechanistic controllability, reframing an LLM's own filler from stylistic noise into a self-regulated computational resource. The buffer-request signal is defined concretely as a difference-in-means direction over about-to-emit-filler versus about-to-emit-substantive step-boundary states, read by a probe and manipulated by steering/patching. We pre-register a dissociation from generic long-form CoT length and from surprisal/entropy so the effect is not mere verbosity, and we test settings where spontaneous filler occurs WITHOUT permissive prompting to show the behavior is native, not prompt-induced. Practically, a buffer-request probe enables adaptive inference-time compute (spend extra tokens only where the model requests buffer) and CoT-safety monitoring of hidden computation; we benchmark the buffer-gated controller against uncertainty-triggered extra-token and repeated-sampling/test-time-scaling baselines, not only random gating.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - Spontaneous filler follows a just-in-time allocation law): Tests that the model raises its own semantically-empty filler at exactly the reasoning points where extra computation is needed, concentrating just before hard sub-computations rather than uniformly. Data: free-form generations over difficulty-graded tasks - a GSM8K/MATH subset (~300 items) selected across operand/step-count difficulty, deductive logic chains depth 2-6 (~300 built), and 2WikiMultiHop-style multi-hop QA (~300 sampled); ~900 items total. Traces are segmented into spans, each auto-classified as SEMANTICALLY-EMPTY FILLER (hedges 'well/hmm/let me think', pure restatements, meta-commentary, contentless discourse connectives) vs SUBSTANTIVE (introduces a new fact/operation/value), using a rubric plus an entailment-based information-gain check, validated against human labels on a 300-span sample (target agreement >=0.8). We use existing task items but must construct the span-level filler annotation because none exists. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; temperature 0.7, 3 seeds (13/21/42). Decisive metric: per-step spontaneous filler rate as a function of local step difficulty, modeled as filler_rate ~ local_step_difficulty + step_position + trace_length + (1|model) + (1|item), where difficulty is proxied by per-step surprisal, operation complexity, and hop index; plus a lead-lag test (does filler at step t predict a hard computation at t+1?). Convincing result: filler rate rises with local step difficulty (coefficient CI excluding 0) beyond length/position, and the lead-lag test shows filler significantly precedes hard sub-computations (CI excluding 0) - a just-in-time allocation signature, not uniform verbosity. Indecision band: a positive but weak difficulty coefficient (CI grazing 0), or filler that co-occurs with but does not lead hard steps - allocation is suggestive only. Negative result: no difficulty dependence or no lead-lag structure - spontaneous filler is uniform stylistic noise, not adaptive allocation.

Experiment 2 (H1 - Causal difficulty check): Tests that injecting a hard sub-step makes the model spontaneously emit more filler just before it. Data/protocol: on items solved correctly under free generation, prompt-inject a controlled hard sub-step vs a matched easy sub-step at a fixed point; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: difference in spontaneous filler emitted immediately before the injected hard vs easy sub-step. Convincing result: the model emits significantly more filler before the hard sub-step than the easy one (paired difference CI excluding 0), establishing difficulty causes allocation rather than merely correlating with it. Indecision band: a small positive difference (CI grazing 0) - weak causal evidence. Negative result: no difference - difficulty does not drive spontaneous filler emission.

Experiment 3 (H2 - Endogenous filler is load-bearing, dissociated from substantive and neutral padding): Tests that the model's own filler carries hidden computation whereas length-matched substantive or neutral padding does not. Data/protocol: (a) answer-emergence - train logit-lens/linear probes to track when the answer becomes decodable across the trace and test whether decodability jumps ACROSS endogenous filler spans more than across length-matched substantive spans; (b) deletion/corruption - remove or scramble the model's own filler spans and re-run continuation from that point, versus removing equal-length substantive-restatement spans, plus a NEUTRAL-FILLER SWAP (replace emitted filler with generic '...' of equal length) to separate specific filler content from mere buffer length; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: accuracy drop when buffer-filler is removed at hard steps, contrasted with the drop from removing matched substantive spans and from the neutral-'...' swap; plus the answer-emergence jump across filler vs substantive spans. Convincing result: removing endogenous filler at hard steps lowers accuracy by >=5 pp more than removing equal-length substantive spans (CI excluding 0), the answer becomes more decodable specifically across filler spans, and the neutral-'...' swap recovers a substantial share of the accuracy (showing buffer length matters) while the model's specific filler adds further benefit. Indecision band: a 2-5 pp differential deletion effect, or an ambiguous neutral-swap result - filler is weakly or non-specifically load-bearing. Negative result: filler deletion hurts no more than substantive-span deletion, and neutral-'...' fully substitutes - endogenous filler carries no special computation, and any buffer benefit is generic to injected padding, dissociating LLMs from the human load-driven-disfluency account.

Experiment 4 (H3 - A locatable buffer-request signal that predicts filler and under-allocation errors, with mediation): Tests that a hidden-state signal governs where filler is emitted. Data/protocol: contrast step-boundary hidden states where the model is about-to-emit filler vs about-to-emit substantive content; per-layer L2-regularized linear probe (3 seeds, 70/30 item-disjoint split) predicting impending filler emission; a difference-in-means buffer-request direction; baselines token entropy and surprisal; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: held-out AUROC for impending filler emission (chance 0.5), whether the signal fires more at hard steps, and whether low buffer-request signal at hard steps predicts errors (under-allocation), beyond entropy/surprisal. Convincing result: best-layer AUROC >=0.75 with incremental value over entropy/surprisal, the signal is elevated at hard steps, low signal at hard steps predicts errors (rho >=0.30, CI excluding 0), and per-item signal predicts filler placement which in turn predicts correctness (mediation). Indecision band: AUROC 0.65-0.75 or mediation rho 0.15-0.30, or no advantage over surprisal - a signal that is real but not distinctly a buffer-request. Negative result: AUROC <0.65 or fully explained by surprisal - no locatable buffer-request signal.

Experiment 5 (H3 - Causal steering and a buffer-gated efficiency controller): Tests that steering the buffer-request signal moves filler and accuracy, and that gating filler by the signal is efficient. Data/protocol: steer +buffer-request at hard steps to induce filler and -buffer-request to suppress it, 4 coefficients; controls random-direction, no-steer, and blanket injected-'...'; then build a Buffer-Gated Generation controller that allows filler only at probe-flagged hard steps and compare accuracy-vs-token-cost against free generation, blanket 'think step by step', and random-gated filler; same five frozen models; specificity tracked on easy-step accuracy and fluency. Decisive metric: accuracy change under +/- buffer-request steering versus no-steer/random, and the accuracy-per-token curve of Buffer-Gated Generation versus baselines. Convincing result: +buffer-request steering at hard steps raises accuracy by >=4 pp (monotonic dose-response), -buffer-request lowers it, random-direction and blanket-'...' move <2 pp, easy-step accuracy and fluency are preserved, and Buffer-Gated Generation matches free-generation accuracy at strictly lower token cost (or higher accuracy at equal cost) versus random-gating. Indecision band: a 2-4 pp steering effect, or a controller that only ties (not beats) random-gating - causal/efficiency signal present but weak. Negative result: <2 pp steering effect or no controller advantage over random-gating - the buffer-request signal is not causally load-bearing and self-buffering confers no controllable benefit.


Adaptive-compute baselines and power: Experiment 5's Buffer-Gated Generation is compared against uncertainty-triggered extra-token allocation and standard repeated-sampling/test-time-scaling at matched token budgets (in addition to random-gating and blanket '...'); all experiments pre-register sample sizes per task/model, primary endpoints, and multiple-comparison correction, and auto-classified filler spans are human-validated as semantically empty (not covert planning text). We report base-vs-instruction-tuned failure cases and keep the two narratives separate — a behavioral allocation law and a candidate mechanistic signal — rather than presenting either as established by the other's evidence.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Classifying spans as semantically-empty filler vs substantive is hard and noisy; mitigated by a rubric + entailment-based information-gain check, human validation on a sample, and multiple detectors, plus reliance on the DELETION and answer-emergence causal tests that do not depend on perfect labels. (2) The adaptive-allocation correlation could be an artifact: hard steps are surprising, and surprisal drives both filler and difficulty; mitigated by the lead-lag test (filler PRECEDES the hard computation), the causal hard-step-injection test, and controlling for length/position. (3) Endogenous filler may simply co-occur with more thinking without being load-bearing; the buffer-vs-substantive and neutral-'...'-swap dissociations, plus deletion/corruption, isolate whether the model's specific filler carries computation. (4) Instruction-tuned models may emit little spontaneous filler (trained toward concise CoT), flattening the effect; we include base variants, less-aligned models, permissive prompts, and tasks where filler naturally appears — low spontaneous filler with a still-present buffer-request signal is itself informative. (5) The buffer-request direction may entangle with generic difficulty/verbosity rather than a specific allocation signal; mitigated by matched about-to-filler/about-to-substantive contrasts, held-out validation, random-direction steering, and easy-step specificity checks. (6) Deletion/re-run changes context and could hurt for trivial reasons; we use matched substantive-span deletion and neutral-swap controls to isolate the buffer-specific effect. (7) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (8) A null result (spontaneous filler is uniform, non-load-bearing, or indistinguishable from injected filler) is itself informative — it would show LLM filler is stylistic noise and that the computation-buffer benefit only exists for experimenter-injected tokens, dissociating LLMs from the human load-driven-disfluency account. (9) The 'self-allocated buffer / disfluency under load' framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like processing.

Name: register_gated_competence
Title: Speaking Down to the Model: Does Colloquial Register Silently Lock an LLM Out of Its Own Competence?
Short Hypothesis: Holding language and semantic content constant, phrasing a problem in a low/colloquial register (slang, texting style, non-standard grammar) versus a high/formal register systematically suppresses an LLM's reasoning competence, and this register penalty is NOT explained by comprehension failure but by the model entering a 'casual/low-effort' processing mode; this mode is a locatable, steerable internal signal, so the model demonstrably possesses the competence but is locked out of it by the register of the surface form.
Related Work: Prior work on surface-form brittleness studies paraphrase robustness generically (Paraphrase and Solve/SCoP, 2024; my prior canonicalization_convergence proposal treated meaning-preserving paraphrase clusters), syntactic complexity of the INPUT (Syntactic Blind Spots, 2025), and multilingual/pivot effects on reasoning (Do Multilingual LLMs Think in English?, 2025). Sociolinguistic register/style is studied for detection and generation (style transfer, formality classifiers) and for bias against non-standard dialects (dialect prejudice in LLMs, 2024), but that work targets fairness/toxicity, not whether register GATES reasoning COMPETENCE. No prior work (a) isolates the high-vs-low register axis while holding language and content fixed as a reasoning-competence manipulation, (b) dissociates a register penalty from comprehension (showing competence is present but inaccessible), or (c) locates and steers a 'processing-register/effort mode' that mediates it. My prior proposals covered language choice, word order, morphology, evidentiality, tense, and paraphrase canonicalization, but never sociolinguistic register as a competence gate. This is distinct: register is orthogonal to language, meaning, and syntactic difficulty, and the claim is that a socially-coded but logically-irrelevant surface cue silently degrades reasoning. We concede that the raw low-register reasoning penalty is largely prior art (register-shift and dialect-prejudice studies, e.g. ReDial/EnDive-style evaluations); our delta is mechanistic, not a new benchmark result. Those works show non-standard phrasing lowers accuracy but never test restatement recovery, a formalize-then-solve two-step, or mediation/patching of a processing-mode representation. Novelty locus: the comprehension-vs-mode DISSOCIATION (competence present but locked out) plus CAUSAL steering/patching of a located register-mode direction. Register is defined operationally as the formal/casual style axis and separated by ablation from dialect, verbosity, slang, tokenization, and grammatical noise.
Abstract: Humans code-switch between a formal 'high' register and a casual 'low' register, and the register we hear shapes how carefully we assume the speaker is thinking. We ask whether large language models inherit an analogous, logically-unwarranted coupling: does phrasing a problem casually make the model reason worse, even though the content is identical? We hypothesize a register-gated competence effect. Holding language and semantics fixed, we rewrite reasoning problems in a high/formal register (standard grammar, precise, professional) versus a low/colloquial register (slang, texting abbreviations, non-standard grammar, filler). We predict low-register phrasing lowers reasoning accuracy relative to high-register phrasing, that this penalty is largest on genuinely hard items, and crucially that it is NOT a comprehension failure: the model can restate the low-register problem correctly and, when forced or steered into a formal processing mode, recovers the lost accuracy, demonstrating the competence was present but locked out. Mechanistically, we test whether the model carries a 'processing-register/effort' signal that low register engages: a probe reads formal-vs-casual mode from hidden states before reasoning and predicts the penalty, and steering along a located register-mode direction (or patching the formal-mode representation) rescues low-register accuracy while suppressing it induces the penalty on formally-phrased items. We evaluate on math, logic, and multi-hop QA across several open-weight models, plus a high-stakes clinical instance where a patient's casual, colloquial description of symptoms silently degrades diagnostic accuracy relative to a clinician's formal chart phrasing of the identical facts. Our work reframes register from a stylistic surface feature into a controllable gate on machine reasoning. The settings that care most are clinical intake, tutoring, consumer support, and low-literacy or code-switched interfaces, where users naturally speak casually; we frame the result as an actionable robustness/fairness diagnostic and measure downstream consequences beyond accuracy — unsafe-advice and refusal rates and calibration error — not just a sociolinguistic curiosity. We use 'competence' only insofar as the restatement, two-step-recovery, and steering/patching dissociations support it; if register does not gate reasoning once content is controlled, the finding is a reassuring null about register-invariance.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 - A register penalty, isolated from length and largest on hard items): Tests that low/colloquial register lowers reasoning accuracy versus high/formal register when content and answer are held constant. Data: a register-paired battery, ~250 items each across three families (~750): multi-step arithmetic/GSM-style (adapted from GSM8K), deductive logic chains depth 2-6 (built), and 2WikiMultiHop-style multi-hop QA (sampled). For each item a HIGH-register rendering (standard formal English) and a LOW-register rendering (colloquial: slang, texting abbreviations 'u/ur/gonna', dropped articles, filler 'like/basically', non-standard grammar) preserve exact content and answer, generated via templated transforms plus an LLM stylizer and VERIFIED meaning-preserving by back-translation, an entailment check, and human spot-checks. An INTERMEDIATE register and a length-matched padded-formal control separate register from length. We construct because no existing set pairs identical reasoning content across a controlled register axis; 250/family keeps meaning-preservation verification affordable. Models: Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; temperature 0.7, 3 seeds (13/21/42). Decisive metric: accuracy, modeled as accuracy ~ register * item_difficulty + (1|model) + (1|item). Convincing result: LOW register lowers accuracy versus HIGH by >=5 pp (main-effect CI excluding 0), the gap widens on harder items (register x difficulty interaction CI excluding 0), and the padded-formal control shows <2 pp change (isolating register from length/verbosity). Indecision band: a 2-5 pp register gap, or an interaction CI grazing 0 - a directional penalty that is not established. Negative result: <2 pp gap, or a padded-formal control that shows the same drop - reasoning is register-invariant (any behavioral penalty is length/tokenization, not register).

Experiment 2 (H1 - Comprehension dissociation and two-step recovery): The key claim that the penalty is a processing-mode gate, not a comprehension failure - the competence is present but locked out. Data/protocol: on the same LOW-register items, measure (a) whether the model can accurately RESTATE/formalize the problem (comprehension check) and (b) on items it restates correctly but answers wrong, whether failure is register-driven rather than misunderstanding; add a TWO-STEP prompt (first formalize, then solve) and test recovery; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: the gap between restatement accuracy and answer accuracy on LOW-register items, and the fraction of the register penalty recovered by the two-step prompt. Convincing result: high restatement accuracy (>=90% of HIGH-register answer accuracy) coexists with low LOW-register answer accuracy - competence present, access blocked - and the two-step formalize-then-solve prompt recovers >=60% of the register penalty (CI excluding 0), pinning the effect on processing mode rather than understanding. Indecision band: partial dissociation (restatement only modestly above answer accuracy) or 30-60% two-step recovery - the comprehension-vs-mode account is not clean. Negative result: restatement accuracy tracks answer accuracy (both low) and two-step gives little recovery - the penalty is genuine comprehension difficulty, refuting the locked-out-competence claim.

Experiment 3 (H2 - A locatable processing-register/effort mode that mediates the penalty): Tests that a formal-vs-casual mode is decodable before reasoning and predicts the per-item penalty. Data/protocol: contrast pre-answer hidden states on HIGH vs LOW renderings (matched content); per-layer L2-regularized linear probe (3 seeds, 70/30 item-disjoint split) decoding formal-vs-casual mode; a difference-in-means formal-mode direction; same five frozen models. Decisive metric: held-out per-layer AUROC for formal-vs-casual mode (chance 0.5), and the Spearman correlation between per-item casual-mode engagement and per-item accuracy drop. Convincing result: best-layer AUROC >=0.80, low register engages a distinct casual mode, and mode engagement predicts the per-item penalty (rho >=0.30, CI excluding 0), mediating register->accuracy. Indecision band: AUROC 0.65-0.80 or mediation rho 0.15-0.30 - a mode representation exists but its link to the penalty is tentative. Negative result: AUROC <0.65 or no engagement-penalty link - no locatable processing-mode signal to explain a behavioral penalty.

Experiment 4 (H3 - Causal rescue via steering and patching): Tests that manipulating the formal-mode representation rescues low-register accuracy and induces the penalty on formal items, holding content fixed. Data/protocol: (a) steering - +formal-mode on LOW-register items and -formal-mode on HIGH-register items, 4 coefficients; controls random-direction and no-steer. (b) patching - cache the pre-reasoning representation from the HIGH-register version and patch it into the LOW-register forward pass before any solution content; specificity via cross-item and random-matched patches. Same five frozen models; specificity tracked on HIGH-register accuracy and fluency. Decisive metric: change in LOW-register accuracy under +formal-mode steering and under HIGH->LOW patching, versus no-steer/random. Convincing result: +formal-mode steering raises LOW-register accuracy toward the HIGH-register level by >=4 pp (monotonic dose-response), -formal-mode induces the penalty on HIGH-register items, HIGH->LOW patching rescues LOW-register accuracy while cross-item/random patches do not (<1.5 pp), random-direction moves <2 pp, and HIGH-register accuracy and fluency are preserved. Indecision band: a 2-4 pp rescue or patching that partly overlaps the random control - causal contribution present but not clean. Negative result: <2 pp rescue or no better than random - the formal-mode direction is not causally responsible for the penalty.

Experiment 5 (H1/H3 - High-stakes clinical instance): Tests that colloquial patient phrasing silently degrades diagnosis and that formal-mode intervention reduces misdiagnosis. Data: ~250 register-paired clinical vignettes where identical diagnostic facts are phrased colloquially (patient-reported, casual) vs formally (clinician chart); adapted from MedQA/MedMCQA stems, meaning-preservation verified. Protocol: same five frozen models; compare colloquial vs formal phrasing and formal-mode steering/patching on fine-distinction cases; aggregate reporting only. Decisive metric: diagnostic misdiagnosis rate on fine-distinction cases as a function of register, and its reduction under intervention. Convincing result: colloquial phrasing raises misdiagnosis by >=6 pp over formal phrasing of identical facts, and formal-mode steering/patching cuts the colloquial misdiagnosis rate by >=6 pp without harming formal-phrasing matched cases. Indecision band: a 2-6 pp register effect or reduction - safety-relevant but modest. Negative result: no register effect on diagnosis, or <2 pp reduction - the register gate does not manifest as a controllable clinical hazard, bounding its practical reach.


Register-isolation ablations and downstream measures: Experiment 1 adds controls separating register from length, sentiment/politeness, lexical rarity, punctuation, dialect, and instruction tone (each varied independently while holding content fixed), with semantic equivalence validated by back-translation, entailment, and human spot-checks on all paired prompts; the mediation test and its falsification condition (no engagement-penalty link) are pre-registered; and Experiment 5 additionally reports refusal rate, unsafe-advice rate, and calibration under colloquial versus formal phrasing so the clinical stakes are quantified beyond raw accuracy.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) Low-register renderings may not be perfectly meaning-preserving, confounding register with subtle content change; mitigated by back-translation, entailment checks, human spot-checks, and templated minimal transforms. (2) The penalty could reflect genuine comprehension difficulty rather than a processing-mode gate; the comprehension/restatement dissociation, the two-step (formalize-then-solve) recovery, and the causal formal-mode steering/patching (which hold content fixed) are designed precisely to distinguish these. (3) Register may confound with token length or tokenization of slang; addressed by the length-matched padded-formal control and by testing that the effect tracks register, not length. (4) Instruction-tuned models may be robust to register, flattening the effect (ceiling); we include harder items, base variants, an intermediate register, and multiple models - a penalty concentrated on hard items is still informative. (5) The formal-mode direction may entangle with generic difficulty/confidence rather than register per se; mitigated by content-matched high/low contrasts, held-out probe validation, random-direction steering, and high-register specificity checks. (6) Patching could rescue by leaking answer content; we patch only the pre-reasoning problem representation (no solution tokens) with cross-item/random specificity controls. (7) Effects may be small or model-specific; we test multiple models and report effect sizes with CIs. (8) A null result (register does not gate competence once content is controlled) is itself informative, showing LLM reasoning is register-invariant and that any behavioral penalty is pure comprehension. (9) The register/diglossia framing is operationalized behaviorally and mechanistically, not as a claim of human-like sociolinguistic cognition; clinical experiments run in controlled research settings with aggregate reporting only.
